orig_differentiation_derivatives.description: Read a derivative as a local gradient, rewrite expressions into powers you can differentiate, and include every inner derivative when a function has more than one layer.

sections.title: What does a derivative tell me?
sections.label: Local gradient and rate
sections.intro:
A derivative gives the local rate of change of a function. On the graph \(y=f(x)\), it is the tangent gradient at a point when a finite derivative exists. Write it as \(f^{\prime}(x)\) or \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).

A chord joins two points on the curve. Its gradient is an average over an interval; as the second point approaches the first, the chord gradients approach the tangent gradient when the derivative exists.

blocks.html:
\[\text{Chord gradient}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\qquad(h\ne0).\]

The limiting tangent gradient is \(f^{\prime}(a)\). The value \(f(a)\) is a height; \(f^{\prime}(a)\) is a gradient. This picture explains the meaning of differentiation; the rules below calculate derivatives directly.
For \(y=x^2\) at \(A=(1,1)\), the chord gradient is \(2+h\). As \(h\) approaches zero from either side, it approaches the tangent gradient \(2\).

blocks.title: A chord gradient and a tangent gradient are different
blocks.prompt: On \(y=x^2\), find the gradient of the chord joining the points with \(x=1\) and \(x=1.2\). The derivative is \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x\); find the tangent gradient at \(x=1\).
blocks.hint: The chord uses the change in height divided by the change in input. The tangent gradient uses the derivative at the stated point.
blocks.solution:
1. \[m_{\mathrm{chord}}=\frac{1.2^2-1^2}{1.2-1}=\frac{0.44}{0.2}=2.2.\]
  2. \[m_{\mathrm{tangent}}=2(1)=2.\]

  3. The finite chord interval gives an average gradient. The tangent gives the local gradient at its first point.

blocks.html: A positive derivative means a positive local slope; a negative derivative means a negative local slope. If the function measures distance in metres and the input is time in seconds, its derivative has units of metres per second.

sections.title: How do I differentiate constants, powers and sums?
sections.label: The power rule

blocks.html:
\[\frac{d}{dx}(ax^n)=anx^{n-1}.\]

Here \(a\) and \(n\) are constants. Multiply by the exponent, then subtract one from the exponent. Use the rule where the real function is differentiable.

\[\frac{d}{dx}(c)=0,\qquad\frac{d}{dx}(ax)=a.\]

Differentiate a sum or difference one term at a time.

For this course, the power rule includes positive integer, negative and rational exponents. A parameter described as constant stays constant during differentiation. Do not differentiate the numerical coefficient separately and discard it.

blocks.title: Differentiate each polynomial term
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=3x^4-2x^2+6x-9\), write \(f^{\prime}(x)=Ax^3+Bx+C\). Find \(A,B,C\).

retry.feedback: The constant \(-9\) contributes zero. The new constant comes from differentiating \(6x\).

blocks.hint: Multiply each coefficient by its exponent and reduce that exponent by one. The constant differentiates to zero.

blocks.html: The new exponent is \(n-1\), including when \(n\) is negative. For \(x^{-2}\), the derivative is \(-2x^{-3}\), not \(-2x^{-1}\). A constant term becomes zero; a linear term becomes its coefficient.
If a polynomial is given as a product, expanding it can make the power rule immediately usable. For example, \((x^2-1)(x+2)=x^3+2x^2-x-2\), whose derivative is \(3x^2+4x-1\).

sections.title: How do I handle roots, fractions and original domains?
sections.label: Rewrite before differentiating

blocks.html:
\[\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad\frac{1}{x^q}=x^{-q},\qquad\frac{x^p}{x^q}=x^{p-q}\quad(x\ne0).\]

Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers, simplify the algebra, then differentiate. Keep the domain of the original expression.

blocks.title: Rewrite roots and reciprocals before differentiating
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=6\sqrt{x}+\frac{4}{x^2}\), where \(x>0\), write \(f^{\prime}(x)=Ax^{-\frac{1}{2}}+Bx^{-3}\). Find \(A,B\) and \(f^{\prime}(1)\).

retry.feedback: The exponent of the reciprocal is \(-2\), so multiplying by it gives a negative coefficient.

blocks.hint: Rewrite the function as \(6x^{\frac{1}{2}}+4x^{-2}\).

blocks.html:
An even root requires a nonnegative radicand; a denominator must be nonzero. The derivative formula may have a smaller domain. For example, \(\sqrt{x}\) is real at zero, but \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\) does not give a finite derivative there.

Odd real roots allow negative inputs. For \(f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}=x^{\frac{1}{3}}\), the derivative is \(\frac{1}{3}x^{-\frac{2}{3}}\) for \(x\ne0\); there is no finite derivative at zero.

Do not simplify \(\sqrt{x^2}\) to \(x\) without a sign condition: it equals \(|x|\). Also, cancelling a denominator does not fill an original hole. For \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\), the function and its derivative \(1\) still exclude \(x=1\).

sections.title: How do I differentiate a power of another expression?
sections.label: The chain rule
sections.intro: A composite function has an outside function applied to an inside expression. For example, in \((2x^2+1)^3\), the inside expression is \(2x^2+1\) and the outside operation is cubing.

blocks.html:
\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\frac{du}{dx}.\]\[y=[g(x)]^n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{dy}{dx}=n[g(x)]^{n-1}g^{\prime}(x).\]

Differentiate the outside while keeping the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
For \(y=(2x^2+1)^3\), the two derivative factors are \(3u^2\) and \(4x\). Substituting back gives \(12x(2x^2+1)^2\).

blocks.title: Include the derivative of the inside expression
blocks.prompt: For \(y=(3x^2-2)^4\), write \(\frac{dy}{dx}=Ax(3x^2-2)^p\). Find \(A,p\) and the derivative at \(x=1\).

retry.feedback: You have differentiated the outer fourth power. Also multiply by the inner derivative \(6x\).

blocks.hint: The outside derivative is \(4(3x^2-2)^3\). Multiply it by the inside derivative \(6x\).

blocks.title: A reciprocal square root has a negative fractional power
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4x+1}}\), write \(f^{\prime}(x)=A(4x+1)^p\). Find \(A,p\), and choose the real domain on which the function and its finite derivative are defined.
blocks.hint: Write the function as \((4x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\), then use the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}(4x+1)^{-\frac{3}{2}}(4)=-2(4x+1)^{-\frac{3}{2}}.\]

  2. The denominator contains a real square root, so \(4x+1>0\). Thus \(x>-\frac{1}{4}\).

blocks.html: The outer power rule alone is incomplete. Keep the sign and coefficient of \(g^{\prime}(x)\), and replace any temporary variable \(u\) with its expression in \(x\) before giving the final answer.

For a linear inside expression, this becomes \(\frac{d}{dx}(ax+b)^n=an(ax+b)^{n-1}\). The same chain method works for a differentiable nonlinear inside expression; its derivative need not be constant.

sections.title: What does differentiating twice mean?
sections.label: Second derivatives

blocks.html:
\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f^{\prime}(x)\bigr)=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.\]

The second derivative is the derivative of the gradient function. It is not \((f^{\prime}(x))^2\).

blocks.title: Differentiate the first derivative again
blocks.prompt: For \(y=2x^3-\frac{5}{x}\), where \(x\ne0\), write \(y^{\prime}=6x^2+Ax^{-2}\) and \(y^{\prime\prime}=12x+Bx^{-3}\). Find \(A,B\) and \(y^{\prime\prime}(1)\).
blocks.hint: Rewrite \(-\frac{5}{x}\) as \(-5x^{-1}\). Repeat the power rule on the whole first derivative.

blocks.html:
For an affine inner expression, applying the chain rule twice gives

\[\frac{d^2}{dx^2}(ax+b)^n=a^2n(n-1)(ax+b)^{n-2},\]

where the function is twice differentiable. For \(n=0\) or \(n=1\), differentiate the constant or linear expression directly: the second derivative is zero.
Show the first derivative before the second. Keep unrounded exact coefficients, reapply every required chain factor, and substitute a requested input only after obtaining the appropriate derivative.

glossary.definition: The local rate of change, equal to a finite tangent gradient when it exists.
A line through two distinct points on a curve.
A line with the curve’s local gradient at a specified point.
The derivative expressed as a function of the input.
A function formed by applying an outside function to an inside expression.
The rate of change of the inside expression, multiplied in the chain rule.
The derivative of the first derivative.
Having a finite derivative at the point under consideration.

examples.title: Move a second point toward a fixed point
examples.question: On \(y=x^2\), keep \(A=(1,1)\) fixed and take \(B=(1+h,(1+h)^2)\), with \(h\ne0\). Compare chord gradients for \(h=1,0.1,-0.1\).
solution: As the second point approaches the first from either side, these gradients approach \(2\). The tangent gradient at \(x=1\) is \(2\).
The point’s height is \(f(1)=1\), while its local gradient is \(f^{\prime}(1)=2\). They describe different features of the curve.

examples.title: Find the gradient function before evaluating it
examples.question: For \(f(x)=2x^4-3x^3+5x-7\), find \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and then \(f^{\prime}(-1)\).
solution: Differentiate first, then substitute the input. Replacing \(x\) with \(-1\) in the original function first would give a single height, not its gradient.

examples.title: Divide each numerator term before using the power rule
examples.question: Differentiate \(y=\frac{2x^3-5x^2+4}{x^2}\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: The division has become a sum of powers, so differentiating term by term is enough. The original zero restriction remains.

examples.title: Use rational and negative exponents in the same derivative
examples.question: For \(y=4\sqrt{x}-\frac{3}{x}\), with \(x>0\), find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and its value at \(x=4\).
solution: The square root and the denominator together require \(x>0\). The derivative is valid on that domain.

examples.title: Differentiate the outer layer and multiply by the inner derivative
examples.question: Differentiate \(y=(2x^2+1)^3\).
solution: The answer is in terms of \(x\), and the inner derivative \(4x\) is included.

examples.title: A decreasing inner function changes the derivative sign
examples.question: Differentiate \(f(x)=\sqrt{5-2x}\), and state where this formula gives a finite real derivative.
solution: The function is real for \(x\le\frac{5}{2}\). Its displayed derivative is finite for \(x<\frac{5}{2}\); at the endpoint the denominator is zero and no finite gradient is obtained.

examples.title: The chain rule is needed again in a second derivative
examples.question: Find the first and second derivatives of \(y=(3x-1)^4\).
solution:
Differentiate the first derivative, including a fresh factor of \(3\) from the inside expression:

\[y^{\prime\prime}=12\cdot3(3x-1)^2(3)=108(3x-1)^2.\]
The second derivative is not the square of the first derivative. It measures how the gradient function changes.

examples.title: Expand a polynomial before taking its second derivative
examples.question: Find \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\) for \(f(x)=(x^2+2)^3\), using powers of \(x\).
solution: The chain rule also gives \(f^{\prime}(x)=6x(x^2+2)^2\). Expanding that polynomial before differentiating again gives the same second derivative without needing a new rule for products.

extraPractice.title: Differentiate before substituting
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=5x^4-3x^2+7x-9\). Write \(f^{\prime}(x)=Ax^3+Bx+C\). Find \(A,B,C\) and the gradient at \(x=-1\).
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate each term. The constant disappears; the linear term gives a constant derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=20x^3-6x+7.\]
  2. \[f^{\prime}(-1)=20(-1)^3-6(-1)+7=-7.\]

  3. The negative derivative means the tangent falls from left to right at this point.

extraPractice.title: Rewrite a quotient as separate powers
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), let \(y=\frac{6x^3-4x+2}{x^2}\). Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}=A+Bx^{-2}+Cx^{-3}\). Find \(A,B,C\) and the gradient at \(x=2\).
extraPractice.hint: Divide every numerator term by \(x^2\) before differentiating. Subtract the exponents.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[y=6x-4x^{-1}+2x^{-2}\qquad(x\ne0).\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=6+4x^{-2}-4x^{-3}.\]
  3. \[\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=6+\frac{4}{4}-\frac{4}{8}=\frac{13}{2}.\]

  4. The original denominator still excludes \(x=0\).

extraPractice.title: Use fractional and negative powers together
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), let \(y=4\sqrt{x}+\frac{3}{x^2}\). Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}=Ax^{-\frac{1}{2}}+Bx^{-3}\). Find \(A,B\) and the gradient at \(x=4\).
extraPractice.hint: Rewrite \(\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}}\). Multiply by the old exponent and then subtract one from it.

extraPractice.title: Keep the negative inner derivative
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(y=(5-2x)^4\). Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}=A(5-2x)^p\). Find \(A,p\) and the gradient at \(x=1\).

retry.feedback: You differentiated the outer power. Multiply by the inner derivative \(-2\) as well.

extraPractice.hint: The outer derivative supplies \(4(5-2x)^3\). Multiply it by the derivative of the entire inner expression.

extraPractice.title: Separate a function endpoint from its derivative domain
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{3x+4}\) on its real domain. Find \(f^{\prime}(4)\). Select the set of inputs where the curve has a finite two-sided derivative.
extraPractice.hint: The square root permits a zero input, but its derivative has that square root in a denominator.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The function is real when \(3x+4\ge0\), so its domain is \(x\ge-\frac{4}{3}\).

  2. \[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3}{2}(3x+4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3x+4}}\quad\left(x>-\frac{4}{3}\right).\]
  3. \[f^{\prime}(4)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{16}}=\frac{3}{8}.\]

  4. At the endpoint the curve has no finite derivative. A defined function value does not guarantee a finite gradient.

extraPractice.title: Apply the inner derivative on both differentiations
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne\frac{1}{2}\), let \(y=3(2x-1)^{-2}\). Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}=A(2x-1)^p\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=B(2x-1)^q\). Find \(A,p,B,q\).

retry.feedback: The second differentiation needs another inner factor of \(2\).

extraPractice.hint: Each differentiation reduces the exponent by one and introduces another factor of \(2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=3(-2)(2x-1)^{-3}(2)=-12(2x-1)^{-3}.\]
  2. \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=(-12)(-3)(2x-1)^{-4}(2)=72(2x-1)^{-4}.\]

  3. Both derivatives retain the original exclusion \(x\ne\frac{1}{2}\). The second derivative is obtained by differentiating again, not by squaring the first derivative.

starters.title: Use derivative conditions to determine two parameters
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+2x-5\), where \(a,b\) are constants. Given \(f^{\prime}(1)=11\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)=24\), find \(a,b\) and \(f^{\prime}(-1)\).
starters.hint: Differentiate symbolically first. The two conditions produce two simultaneous linear equations in \(a,b\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain both derivative expressions.
  • 1 mark: use the two conditions to obtain both linear equations.
  • 1 mark: solve for \(a=5\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(b=-3\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate the requested gradient as \(23\).

starters.title: Differentiate a nonlinear composition twice
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=(x^2+3)^3\). Use the chain rule to write \(f^{\prime}(x)=Ax(x^2+3)^2\). Find \(A\), \(f^{\prime}(1)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)\). Show a power-rule method for the second derivative on paper.
starters.hint: Multiply the outer derivative by \(2x\). To differentiate again using the rules in this lesson, expand the first derivative into a sum of powers.
starters.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3(x^2+3)^2(2x)=6x(x^2+3)^2.\]
  2. \[f^{\prime}(1)=6(1)(4)^2=96.\]
  3. \[f^{\prime}(x)=6x(x^4+6x^2+9)=6x^5+36x^3+54x.\]
  4. \[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=30x^4+108x^2+54,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(1)=192.\]

  5. All expressions here are defined for every real \(x\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: apply the outer power rule.
  • 1 mark: include the inner factor \(2x\) and obtain \(A=6\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate \(f^{\prime}(1)=96\).
  • 1 mark: expand and differentiate again to obtain \(30x^4+108x^2+54\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)=192\).

starters.title: Keep the domain when rewriting fractional powers
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{2x^2-5x+2}{\sqrt{x}}\). Rewrite \(f\) as a sum of powers, then find \(f^{\prime}(1)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)\). Select the real domain of the original function.
starters.hint: The denominator must be both real and nonzero. Subtract \(\frac{1}{2}\) from each numerator exponent before differentiating.
starters.solution:
1. \[f(x)=2x^{\frac{3}{2}}-5x^{\frac{1}{2}}+2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\qquad(x>0).\]
  2. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{5}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}-x^{-\frac{3}{2}}.\]
  3. \[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{3}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{5}{4}x^{-\frac{3}{2}}+\frac{3}{2}x^{-\frac{5}{2}}.\]
  4. \[f^{\prime}(1)=3-\frac{5}{2}-1=-\frac{1}{2},\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{4}+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{17}{4}.\]

  5. The original domain is \(x>0\); rewriting the expression does not add \(x=0\) or any negative input.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: state the original domain \(x>0\).
  • 1 mark: rewrite all three terms as powers correctly.
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete first derivative.
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete second derivative.
  • 1 mark: evaluate \(f^{\prime}(1)=-\frac{1}{2}\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate \(f^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{17}{4}\).

revision.body:
Rewrite if useful, differentiate, preserve the domain, then substitute.

Meaning and the power rule

\(f(a)\) is the height; \(f^{\prime}(a)\) is the local gradient.

\[\frac{d}{dx}(ax^n)=anx^{n-1},\qquad\frac{d}{dx}(c)=0.\]

Constants stay constant parameters. Differentiate sums term by term; a linear term \(ax\) becomes \(a\).

Rewrite and keep the original domain

\[\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad\frac{1}{x^q}=x^{-q}.\]

Divide a monomial denominator into each numerator term, or expand a polynomial product. Denominators exclude zero; even roots need nonnegative radicands. A derivative may exclude a root endpoint. Odd real roots permit negative inputs. Cancellation does not fill original holes.

The chain rule

\[y=[g(x)]^n\Longrightarrow y^{\prime}=n[g(x)]^{n-1}g^{\prime}(x).\]\[y=(ax+b)^n\Longrightarrow y^{\prime}=an(ax+b)^{n-1}.\]

Keep the inside unchanged while differentiating the outside; then multiply by the inner derivative. Preserve its sign and substitute any temporary variable back.

Second derivatives and checks

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f^{\prime}(x)\bigr)=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.\]

Differentiate again, not square. Use a fresh chain factor when needed; expand a polynomial if that makes the next step simpler. Keep fractions exact. Evaluate the requested derivative only after differentiating, and check its finite real domain.
revision.checks:
• Coefficient multiplied by exponent; exponent reduced by one?
  • Constants and original domain handled?
  • Every inner derivative included?
  • Correct derivative evaluated at the stated input?

orig_differentiation_tangents_normals.description: Use the curve for the contact point and its derivative for the direction. Build the line, keep every valid contact, and treat vertical cases separately.

sections.title: How do I find the tangent at a given input?
sections.label: Point, gradient, line
sections.intro: A tangent at \((a,f(a))\) passes through that contact point and has the curve’s local gradient \(f^{\prime}(a)\), when this is finite. It need not stay on one side of the curve: a tangent can cross a curve.

blocks.html:
\[m_T=f^{\prime}(a),\qquad y-f(a)=m_T(x-a).\]

Use the original function for the contact height and its derivative for the gradient. Then use the point–slope equation of a line.

blocks.title: Use the curve for the height and the derivative for the gradient
blocks.prompt: Find the tangent to \(y=2x^2-x\) at \(x=2\). Give the contact point’s height, the tangent gradient, and its intercept in \(y=mx+c\).
blocks.hint: Substitute \(x=2\) into the curve for the height and into \(4x-1\) for the gradient.

blocks.html: If the contact point is already given, check that it lies on the curve. If only its input is supplied, calculate the missing height before writing the line. A point–slope answer is already a valid line equation unless another form is requested.
Do not use \(f(a)\) as the gradient or \(f^{\prime}(a)\) as the height. Find both separately and label them.

sections.title: How do I find a normal, including a horizontal-tangent case?
sections.label: Normals and exceptions
sections.intro: The normal passes through the same contact point and is perpendicular to the tangent. For finite nonzero tangent gradient, take its negative reciprocal.

blocks.html:
\[m_N=-\frac{1}{m_T}\qquad(m_T\ne0\text{ and finite}).\]\[y-f(a)=-\frac{1}{f^{\prime}(a)}(x-a).\]

With finite nonzero gradients, check \(m_Tm_N=-1\).
At \((1,1)\) on \(y=x^2\), the tangent is \(y=2x-1\), while the normal is \(y=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}\). Both share the contact point.

blocks.title: Use the negative reciprocal for a normal
blocks.prompt: Find the normal to \(y=x^2-x\) at \(x=2\). Write it as \(y=mx+c\) and find \(m,c\).

retry.feedback: Perpendicular gradients are negative reciprocals, not just negatives. Use \(-\frac{1}{3}\).

blocks.hint: The contact point is \((2,2)\), and the tangent gradient is \(3\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[m_T=2(2)-1=3,\qquad m_N=-\frac{1}{3}.\]
  2. \[y-2=-\frac{1}{3}(x-2)\Longrightarrow y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{8}{3}.\]

blocks.html:
If \(m_T=0\), the tangent is horizontal and the normal is vertical:

\[\text{Tangent: }y=f(a),\qquad\text{normal: }x=a.\]

If a genuine vertical tangent exists, its normal is horizontal. An undefined derivative alone does not prove a vertical tangent; a corner can have no unique tangent.

blocks.title: A horizontal tangent has a vertical normal
blocks.prompt: For \(y=(x+1)^2-4\), find the tangent and normal at \(x=-1\). Give the constant in \(y=c\) for the tangent, then choose the normal’s form and give its constant.
blocks.hint: The derivative is \(2(x+1)\), so the tangent gradient at the stated point is zero.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P=(-1,-4),\qquad m_T=0.\]
  2. \[\text{Tangent: }y=-4,\qquad\text{normal: }x=-1.\]

  3. No finite normal gradient is used here; the normal is vertical.

blocks.html: A vertical line has equation \(x=a\), not an infinite coefficient in \(y=mx+c\). Handle it directly rather than dividing by zero.

sections.title: How do I locate every point with a required direction?
sections.label: Prescribed gradients
sections.intro: First translate the line information into the required tangent gradient. Then solve the derivative equation and recover every allowed contact height from the original curve.

blocks.html:
For a given finite nonzero line gradient \(m\):

  • Tangent parallel to the line: solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=m\).
  • Tangent perpendicular to the line: solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{1}{m}\).
  • Normal parallel to the line: the tangent is perpendicular, so solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{1}{m}\).
  • Normal perpendicular to the line: the tangent is parallel, so solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=m\).

For horizontal or vertical given lines, use their directions directly.

blocks.title: Translate perpendicular information before solving
blocks.prompt: Find all points on \(y=x^3-6x\) where the tangent is perpendicular to \(x+6y=5\).
blocks.hint: The given line has gradient \(-\frac{1}{6}\), so the tangent needs gradient \(6\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[3x^2-6=6\Longrightarrow x^2=4\Longrightarrow x=\pm2.\]
  2. \[x=2:\ y=8-12=-4;\qquad x=-2:\ y=-8+12=4.\]

  3. The points are \((2,-4)\) and \((-2,4)\). Both have tangent gradient \(6\), whose product with \(-\frac{1}{6}\) is \(-1\).

blocks.html: Keep all real solutions in the original domain. A reciprocal curve excludes zero; a root expression may restrict the input further. A quadratic gradient equation can give two contact points and therefore two distinct lines.
After solving for the inputs, substitute them into the original curve. The derivative gives the contact inputs, not their heights. A parallel line supplies a gradient, not an intercept.

sections.title: What if the line must pass through another point?
sections.label: Unknown contact points
sections.intro: A point through which the tangent passes is not necessarily the contact point. Introduce an unknown contact input \(a\), build the tangent there, then impose the given point \(A=(u,v)\).

blocks.html:
\[y=f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)(x-a).\]\[\text{Through }(u,v):\quad v=f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)(u-a).\]

Solve this equation for every allowed contact input \(a\). Then write and check each complete tangent.
Two tangents from \((0,-1)\) meet \(y=x^2\) at different contact points, \((-1,1)\) and \((1,1)\). The shared external point is not a contact point.

blocks.title: An external point is not the contact point
blocks.prompt: Find the contact points and gradients of all tangents from \(A=(0,-9)\) to \(y=x^2\).
blocks.hint: Use an unknown contact \((a,a^2)\). Its tangent is \(y=2ax-a^2\), which must pass through \((0,-9)\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[-9=-a^2\Longrightarrow a=\pm3.\]
  2. \[a=3:\ (3,9),\ m=6;\qquad a=-3:\ (-3,9),\ m=-6.\]

  3. The two tangent equations are \(y=6x-9\) and \(y=-6x-9\). Each passes through the external point and its own contact point.

blocks.html: The given point may itself lie on the curve, but another contact may still give a tangent through it. Do not divide by \(u-a\) without checking \(a=u\). Repeated roots count as one contact input; keep every distinct valid root.
For a normal through an external point, use the normal line at the unknown contact. Check horizontal-tangent contacts separately before taking a reciprocal gradient.

sections.title: How do tangency conditions determine unknown parameters?
sections.label: Linked point and gradient conditions
sections.intro: A tangent line gives two kinds of information: its height at the contact input and its gradient. Substitute the point condition into the original curve and the gradient condition into its derivative, then solve the equations together.

blocks.title: Tangency gives a point condition and a gradient condition
blocks.prompt: The line \(y=6x-3\) is tangent to \(y=ax^2+bx+1\) at \(x=2\). Find \(a,b\).
blocks.hint: The line gives contact height \(9\) at \(x=2\), and its gradient is \(6\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[4a+2b+1=9\Longrightarrow2a+b=4.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=2ax+b,\qquad4a+b=6.\]

  3. Subtract the first simplified equation from the second: \(2a=2\), so \(a=1\) and \(b=2\).

  4. The curve gives height \(9\) and gradient \(6\) at \(x=2\), so both tangency conditions hold.

blocks.html:
At a shared contact input \(a\), two differentiable curves \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\) have the same tangent if

\[f(a)=g(a),\qquad f^{\prime}(a)=g^{\prime}(a).\]

Equal gradients alone only establish parallel directions; the lines must also pass through the same point to be identical.

Verify the final line passes through each stated point and has the correct tangent or normal direction at its contact. In a parameter problem, check both the original curve equation and the derivative condition.

glossary.definition: The point on the curve at which the tangent and normal are being constructed.
A line through the contact point with the curve’s local direction there.
The line through the contact point perpendicular to its tangent.
The perpendicular finite gradient \(-\frac{1}{m}\), defined when \(m\ne0\).
A gradient supplied by the question directly or through a line relation.
A separate point through which the required line must pass; it need not be on the curve.
The line equation \(y-y_0=m(x-x_0)\).

examples.title: Build a tangent from a point and a gradient
examples.question: Find the tangent to \(y=x^2+3x\) at \(x=1\).
solution: Substituting \(x=1\) into the line gives \(y=4\), and its gradient is the required \(5\).

examples.title: A normal shares the contact point but has a different direction
examples.question: Find the normal to \(y=x^2\) at \(P=(1,1)\).
solution: The normal passes through \((1,1)\), and \(2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-1\), so it is perpendicular to the tangent.

examples.title: Handle a zero tangent gradient directly
examples.question: Find the tangent and normal to \(y=x^3-3x\) at \(x=1\).
solution:
The tangent is horizontal through the contact height; the normal is vertical through the contact input.

\[\text{Tangent: }y=-2,\qquad\text{normal: }x=1.\]

examples.title: A prescribed gradient can give more than one contact point
examples.question: Find all tangents to \(y=x^3-3x\) that are parallel to \(y=24x+7\).
solution: Both lines have the prescribed gradient. The given line’s intercept \(7\) is not transferred to the tangents.

examples.title: A prescribed normal gradient determines the tangent gradient
examples.question: Find the normals to \(y=x^3\) that are parallel to \(x+3y=7\).
solution: The given line has gradient \(-\frac{1}{3}\). The normal must have that gradient, so the tangent gradient must be \(3\).

examples.title: Use an unknown contact point for an external tangent
examples.question: Find every tangent from \(A=(0,-1)\) to \(y=x^2\).
solution: Let the contact point be \(P=(a,a^2)\). Its tangent gradient is \(2a\).

Substitute the external point into this line:

\[-1=-a^2\Longrightarrow a=\pm1.\]
The contacts are \((1,1)\) and \((-1,1)\). Both lines pass through \((0,-1)\), which is not on the curve.

examples.title: An external normal problem can include a vertical branch
examples.question: Find all normals to \(y=x^2\) passing through \(A=\left(0,\frac{9}{2}\right)\).
solution: At contact input \(a=0\), the tangent is horizontal and the normal is \(x=0\). It passes through \(A\), so keep this solution before using a reciprocal gradient.
There are three normals: these two sloping lines and the vertical line \(x=0\). Their contact points are \((2,4),(-2,4),(0,0)\).

examples.title: Use both pieces of information in a given tangent line
examples.question: The line \(y=6x-5\) is tangent to \(y=x^2+px+q\) at \(x=2\). Find \(p,q\).
solution:
The line gives the contact height \(6(2)-5=7\). Therefore

\[4+2p+q=7.\]
With \(p=2,q=-1\), the curve has height \(7\) and gradient \(6\) at \(x=2\), matching the given line.
