extraPractice.title: Use the curve value as the ordinate
extraPractice.prompt: Find the tangent to \(y=x^3-4x+1\) at \(x=2\). Write the tangent as \(y=mx+c\), and enter \(m,c\).

retry.feedback: The derivative gives the gradient, not the ordinate. The actual contact is \((2,1)\).

extraPractice.hint: Find the point from the original function and the gradient from its derivative. They are different calculations.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[y(2)=8-8+1=1,\qquad \frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-4.\]
  2. \[m=3(2)^2-4=8.\]
  3. \[y-1=8(x-2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=8x-15.\]

extraPractice.title: Use the negative reciprocal for a normal
extraPractice.prompt: Find the normal to \(y=x^2+2x-3\) at \(x=1\). Write it as \(y=mx+c\), and enter \(m,c\).

retry.feedback: This is the tangent gradient. The normal uses its negative reciprocal.
The reciprocal needs a minus sign: perpendicular finite gradients multiply to \(-1\).

extraPractice.hint: The point is on the curve, while the normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the nonzero tangent gradient.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[y(1)=0,\qquad \frac{dy}{dx}=2x+2,\qquad m_{\mathrm{tan}}=4.\]
  2. \[m_{\mathrm{normal}}=-\frac{1}{4}.\]
  3. \[y=-\frac{1}{4}(x-1)=-\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}.\]

extraPractice.title: Recognise a vertical normal
extraPractice.prompt: At the point on \(y=(x-2)^2+3\) with \(x=2\), choose the correct form for the normal. Give its constant, and give the height of the horizontal tangent.
extraPractice.hint: The tangent gradient is zero. Handle this case directly; do not divide by zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=2(x-2),\qquad \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=0.\]

  2. The point is \((2,3)\), so the horizontal tangent is \(y=3\). The perpendicular normal is vertical:

    \[x=2.\]

extraPractice.title: Find every point with a prescribed tangent direction
extraPractice.prompt: Find all points on \(y=x^3-3x+2\) where the tangent is parallel to \(9x-y+4=0\). Give every contact point and the set of intercepts \(c\) for these tangents in the form \(y=9x+c\).
extraPractice.hint: Rewrite the given line in gradient form. Solve the derivative equation completely, then find each ordinate from the original curve.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[9x-y+4=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=9x+4.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-3=9\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\pm2.\]

  3. The corresponding curve points are \((-2,0)\) and \((2,4)\).

  4. \[y=9(x+2)=9x+18,\qquad y-4=9(x-2)\Longrightarrow y=9x-14.\]

  5. Both tangents have the prescribed gradient. Their different intercepts make them different parallel lines.

extraPractice.title: Translate a normal direction into a tangent condition
extraPractice.prompt: Find every point on \(y=\frac{1}{x}\), with \(x\ne0\), where the normal is parallel to \(y=4x-1\).
extraPractice.hint: The required normal gradient is \(4\), so the tangent gradient must be \(-\frac{1}{4}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{x^2},\qquad -\frac{1}{x^2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\]
  2. \[x^2=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\pm2.\]

  3. Both inputs are in the original domain. The required points are \(\left(-2,-\frac{1}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(2,\frac{1}{2}\right)\). Each tangent has gradient \(-\frac{1}{4}\), so each normal has gradient \(4\).

extraPractice.title: Use separate position and gradient conditions
extraPractice.prompt: The curve \(y=ax^2+bx-2\) passes through \((1,3)\), and its tangent there has gradient \(7\). Find \(a,b\). Then write the normal there as \(y=mx+c\) and find \(m,c\).
extraPractice.hint: The point gives one equation in the function. The direction gives a second equation in its derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[a+b-2=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+b=5.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=2ax+b,\qquad 2a+b=7.\]

  3. Subtracting gives \(a=2\), then \(b=3\).

  4. \[y-3=-\frac{1}{7}(x-1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=-\frac{1}{7}x+\frac{22}{7}.\]

  5. The recovered curve gives \(y(1)=3\) and \(y^{\prime}(1)=7\), confirming both original conditions.

starters.title: Find both tangents from an external point
starters.question: Find every tangent to \(y=x^2+1\) that passes through \((0,-3)\). Give all contact points and write each tangent as \(y=mx+c\). Enter the complete set of ordered pairs \((m,c)\).
starters.hint: Name the unknown contact input \(a\). The contact point is \((a,a^2+1)\), and the tangent gradient is \(2a\). Insert the given external point into that tangent equation.
starters.solution:
1. \[y-(a^2+1)=2a(x-a)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=2ax+1-a^2.\]

  2. Passing through \((0,-3)\) requires

    \[-3=1-a^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a^2=4.\]

  3. Thus \(a=-2\) or \(a=2\), giving contact points \((-2,5)\) and \((2,5)\).

  4. \[y=-4x-3\qquad\text{or}\qquad y=4x-3.\]

  5. Both lines pass through \((0,-3)\), pass through their respective contact points, and have the derivative gradient at those contacts.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the tangent at a variable contact \(a\).
  • 1 mark: use the external point to obtain \(a^2=4\).
  • 1 mark: retain both contact inputs and both correct ordinates.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(y=-4x-3\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(y=4x-3\) and verify both meet the given point.

starters.title: A given point on the curve need not be the only contact
starters.question: Find every tangent to \(y=x^3-3x\) that passes through \(P=(1,-2)\). Although \(P\) lies on the curve, a required tangent may touch elsewhere. Give all contact points and the complete set of line parameters \((m,c)\) for \(y=mx+c\).
starters.hint: The tangent at input \(a\) has equation \(y=(3a^2-3)x-2a^3\). Substitute \(P\), then factor the resulting cubic using the known contact \(a=1\).
starters.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(a)=3a^2-3,\qquad y-(a^3-3a)=(3a^2-3)(x-a).\]
  2. \[y=(3a^2-3)x-2a^3.\]
  3. \[-2=3a^2-3-2a^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2a^3-3a^2+1=0.\]
  4. \[(a-1)^2(2a+1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=1\ \text{or}\ a=-\frac{1}{2}.\]

  5. The repeated algebraic root \(a=1\) is one contact, not two different contacts. At \(a=1\), the tangent is horizontal: \(y=-2\).

  6. At \(a=-\frac{1}{2}\), the ordinate is \(\frac{11}{8}\) and the gradient is \(-\frac{9}{4}\), giving

    \[y=-\frac{9}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}.\]

  7. Substituting \(x=1\) gives \(y=-2\) on each line. Both lines also meet the curve with its derivative gradient at their stated contacts.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the tangent equation at the unknown contact.
  • 1 mark: obtain the contact equation from \(P\).
  • 1 mark: factor the cubic completely.
  • 1 mark: retain the two distinct contact inputs, counting the repeated root only once.
  • 1 mark: obtain both complete contact coordinates.
  • 1 mark: obtain the horizontal tangent \(y=-2\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the other tangent and verify that it passes through \(P\).

starters.title: Recover a reciprocal model from normal information
starters.question: For \(x>0\), the curve \(y=ax^2+\frac{b}{x}\) passes through \((1,5)\). Its normal there has gradient \(-\frac{1}{4}\). Find \(a,b\), then find the normal at the point with \(x=2\), writing it as \(y=mx+c\).
starters.hint: First turn the given normal gradient into the tangent gradient. Combine the derivative condition with the point condition, then repeat the point-and-gradient method at the new input.
starters.solution:
1. \[a+b=5,\qquad \frac{dy}{dx}=2ax-\frac{b}{x^2}.\]

  2. The tangent gradient at \(x=1\) is \(4\), so \(2a-b=4\). Solving the pair gives \(a=3,b=2\).

  3. \[y(2)=3(2)^2+\frac{2}{2}=13,\qquad y^{\prime}(2)=6(2)-\frac{2}{2^2}=\frac{23}{2}.\]
  4. \[m_{\mathrm{normal}}=-\frac{2}{23},\qquad y-13=-\frac{2}{23}(x-2).\]
  5. \[y=-\frac{2}{23}x+\frac{303}{23}.\]

  6. The original conditions are satisfied: \(y(1)=5\), and the tangent gradient \(4\) gives the stated normal gradient \(-\frac{1}{4}\). Both requested inputs are positive.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the point to obtain \(a+b=5\).
  • 1 mark: convert the normal direction and obtain \(2a-b=4\).
  • 1 mark: solve for \(a=3,b=2\).
  • 1 mark: find the new point \((2,13)\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the new normal gradient \(-\frac{2}{23}\).
  • 1 mark: give the complete normal equation.

revision.body:
Find the contact point and gradient separately, then write and check the line.

Tangent and normal at a contact

\[P=(a,f(a)),\qquad m_T=f^{\prime}(a).\]\[\text{Tangent: }y-f(a)=m_T(x-a).\]\[\text{Normal: }m_N=-\frac{1}{m_T}\quad(m_T\ne0\text{ and finite}).\]

Use the same contact point in the normal equation. Check \(m_Tm_N=-1\) when both gradients are finite and nonzero.

Directions and exceptions

Horizontal tangent: \(y=f(a)\); vertical normal: \(x=a\). A genuine vertical tangent has a horizontal normal. Parallel finite gradients are equal; perpendicular nonzero gradients are negative reciprocals.

Solve for every allowed contact input, then find heights using the original curve. Keep its domain restrictions.

A line through another point

\[v=f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)(u-a).\]

This makes the tangent at unknown contact \(a\) pass through \((u,v)\). The given point need not be the contact. Check \(a=u\) before dividing by \(u-a\). Keep distinct roots. For external normals, check zero-gradient contacts separately.

Linked conditions and final checks

Use a given line’s contact height in the original curve and its gradient in the derivative. Solve parameter equations together. Equal curve heights and derivatives at the same input give a common tangent.

Check the final line through every specified point, its direction at the contact and all original restrictions.
revision.checks:
• Contact height from the original curve?
  • Correct tangent or normal direction?
  • All contact roots and vertical exceptions included?
  • Final lines and parameter conditions checked?

orig_differentiation_curve_behaviour.description: Use derivative signs to explain a curve’s direction, locate and classify stationary points, and find the full range on the stated domain.

sections.title: How do derivative signs tell me where a curve rises or falls?
sections.label: Derivative signs
sections.intro: Increasing means that outputs rise as the input moves to the right; decreasing means that they fall. For a differentiable function on an interval, a positive derivative throughout gives strict increase, and a negative derivative throughout gives strict decrease.

blocks.html: Find \(f^{\prime}(x)\), mark its zeros and points where the function or derivative is undefined, then determine its sign on every remaining interval. Factorisation often makes the signs clear. A test value is useful only after you have found all points at which the sign could change.
The signs of \(3(x+1)(x-1)\) explain the rising, falling and rising sections of \(y=x^3-3x\).

blocks.title: Separate zero gradients from negative gradients
blocks.prompt: For \(g(x)=x^3-3x^2-24x\), find all inputs where \(g^{\prime}(x)=0\), then choose the interval where \(g^{\prime}(x)<0\).
blocks.hint: Factor \(g^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-6x-24\). Test the sign in each interval separated by its roots.
blocks.solution:
1. \[g^{\prime}(x)=3(x+2)(x-4)=0\Longrightarrow x=-2,4.\]

  2. The factors have opposite signs between the roots, so \(g^{\prime}(x)<0\) exactly when \(-2<x<4\). At the endpoints the gradient is zero, not negative.

blocks.html: Nonnegative derivative means the function never decreases; it does not by itself guarantee strict increase, since a constant function also has zero derivative. Conversely, strict increase can include isolated zero gradients, as \(x^3\) shows later. If asked where \(f^{\prime}(x)>0\), exclude its zeros; a full increasing interval can still include them.
Keep disconnected domain components separate. A formula with a zero denominator does not define a curve point there, and derivative signs must not be carried across the gap as one interval.

sections.title: How do I find and classify every stationary point?
sections.label: Stationary coordinates
sections.intro: A stationary point has a horizontal tangent: its finite derivative is zero. Solve \(f^{\prime}(x)=0\) within the original domain, then use \(y=f(x)\) to find each height. A turning point is a local maximum or minimum, where the direction changes.

blocks.html:
At an isolated stationary input, compare the derivative signs immediately on either side:

  • Positive then negative: local maximum.
  • Negative then positive: local minimum.
  • The same nonzero sign on both sides: neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Local describes nearby values; it does not compare the point with the whole domain.

blocks.title: Give complete stationary coordinates
blocks.prompt: Find the stationary points of \(h(x)=2x^3-3x^2-12x+5\). Which stationary input gives a local maximum?
blocks.hint: Use \(h^{\prime}(x)=6(x+1)(x-2)\). Substitute its roots into \(h\), then compare derivative signs.
blocks.solution:
1. \[h^{\prime}(x)=0\Longrightarrow x=-1,2.\]
  2. \[h(-1)=12,\qquad h(2)=-15.\]

  3. The derivative signs are positive, negative, positive across the three intervals. Thus \((-1,12)\) is a local maximum and \((2,-15)\) is a local minimum.

blocks.html: When asked for stationary points, give complete coordinates and justify each classification. An input alone is not a point, and \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) alone does not identify a maximum or minimum.

sections.title: When does the second derivative decide the nature?
sections.label: Second derivative test
sections.intro: At a stationary input \(a\), the second derivative gives a quick classification when it is nonzero. First establish \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\); the second derivative is not a substitute for finding stationary inputs.

blocks.html:
\[f^{\prime\prime}(a)>0:\ \text{local minimum};\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(a)<0:\ \text{local maximum}.\]

If \(f^{\prime\prime}(a)=0\), the test is inconclusive. Return to the first-derivative sign test.
At the origin, \(x^4\), \(-x^4\) and \(x^3\) all have zero second derivative, but their stationary points have different natures.

blocks.title: A zero second derivative needs another test
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=4-(x+2)^4\), find \(f^{\prime\prime}(-2)\) and classify the stationary point at \(x=-2\).

options.neither: Neither a maximum nor a minimum

blocks.hint: Inspect the sign of \(-4(x+2)^3\) immediately on either side of \(-2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=-4(x+2)^3,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-12(x+2)^2.\]

  2. At \(x=-2\), both derivatives are zero. The first derivative is positive to the left and negative to the right, so \((-2,4)\) is a maximum.

blocks.html: Zero second derivative does not mean “neither”, and zero first derivative does not necessarily mean a turn. State the actual signs or the nonzero second-derivative value that supports your conclusion.

sections.title: How do domain restrictions change the range?
sections.label: Ranges and endpoints
sections.intro: The range contains every output attained on the stated domain. A global maximum or minimum compares all allowed inputs. For a continuous curve on a closed interval, compare the values at all interior stationary points and both endpoints. Check any interior points where the derivative does not exist as well.

blocks.html: For an open endpoint, determine the value approached and whether it is attained anywhere else. Use a square bracket only for an attained range bound. Continuity fills the values between extrema on each domain component; combine component ranges at the end.

blocks.title: An open domain endpoint can give an unattained bound
blocks.prompt: Find the range of \(f(x)=(x+1)^2-2\) on \(-1<x\le2\). Give the lower and upper bounds and select which are included.
blocks.hint: The derivative is positive throughout this domain. Compare the value approached at the open end with the value at the included end.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=2(x+1)>0\quad\text{for }-1<x\le2.\]

  2. As \(x\) approaches \(-1\) from the right, \(f(x)\) approaches \(-2\), but never equals it. At \(x=2\), \(f(2)=7\).

  3. \[\text{Range: }(-2,7],\qquad -2<f(x)\le7.\]

blocks.html: An endpoint can give an extreme without being stationary. For example, \(y=\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,4]\) has its minimum at \(x=0\), even though \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\) is only finite for \(x>0\). Check the original function at the boundary.

blocks.title: Join the ranges of separate domain components
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=x+\frac{25}{x}\), \(x\ne0\), find the stationary points and choose the full range.
blocks.hint: Study the negative and positive inputs separately. Each component has one stationary point.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=1-\frac{25}{x^2}=0\Longrightarrow x=\pm5.\]
  2. \[f(-5)=-10,\qquad f(5)=10.\]

  3. On the negative component the greatest value is \(-10\), and values decrease without bound near either end. On the positive component the least value is \(10\), and values increase without bound near either end.

  4. \[\text{Range: }(-\infty,-10]\cup[10,\infty).\]

blocks.html: Do not read the entire range from the two stationary heights. Check endpoints, excluded inputs and behaviour toward each end of an unbounded domain. “Local maximum” can coexist with values much larger elsewhere.

sections.title: How do parameters change stationary behaviour?
sections.label: Complete parameter cases
sections.intro: A parameter can alter the number of real stationary inputs or move them outside the allowed domain. Solve the derivative equation before assuming how many points exist. Separate the boundary case where two roots meet from the cases on either side.

blocks.title: Read the parameter sign from this derivative
blocks.prompt: Let \(h(x)=x^3+3kx+1\), where \(k\) is real. Choose the condition for two distinct stationary points, then the condition for strict increase throughout the real line.

fields.label: Strictly increasing for all real inputs

blocks.hint: Here \(h^{\prime}(x)=3(x^2+k)\). Treat the equality case separately.
blocks.solution:
1. \[h^{\prime}(x)=0\Longrightarrow x^2=-k.\]

  2. There are two distinct real roots exactly when \(k<0\). If \(k>0\), the derivative is positive everywhere. If \(k=0\), \(h(x)=x^3+1\) is still strictly increasing, with one zero gradient.

  3. Therefore strict increase throughout the real line holds for \(k\ge0\).

blocks.html: A vertical shift \(f(x)+c\) keeps the same derivatives, stationary inputs and classifications, but adds \(c\) to every height and range bound. If stationary inputs are given in a parameter question, substitute each into \(f^{\prime}(x)=0\); use any stated height in \(f(x)\), then check all original conditions.

Answer a parameter question with complete inequalities, including or excluding the equality case for a stated reason. “Two distinct stationary points” and “strictly increasing” require different checks.

glossary.definition: A point on the curve where the finite derivative is zero.
A local maximum or minimum where a curve changes between increasing and decreasing.
A point whose height is at least as large as nearby curve heights.
A point whose height is at most as large as nearby curve heights.
A greatest or least value over the whole stated domain.
The set of all outputs attained at allowed inputs.
Whenever \(x_1<x_2\) in the interval, \(f(x_1)<f(x_2)\).

examples.title: Turn a derivative into a sign chart
examples.question: Find where \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) has positive or negative gradient. State its increasing and decreasing intervals.
solution: The only zeros are \(-1\) and \(1\). They split the real line into three intervals. The two factors have the same sign outside these roots and opposite signs between them.

The function is strictly increasing on each of \(( -\infty,-1]\) and \([1,\infty)\), and strictly decreasing on \([-1,1]\). Including the zero-gradient endpoints does not spoil these monotonic intervals.

examples.title: A missing input separates two intervals
examples.question: For \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-1}\), determine where the function decreases and whether it has a stationary point.
solution: It is strictly decreasing on \(( -\infty,1)\) and separately on \((1,\infty)\). The derivative is never zero, so there is no stationary point.
The excluded input \(1\) is not a point on the curve. Do not join the intervals across it.
The function is not decreasing across its whole disconnected domain: \(0<2\), but \(f(0)=-1<f(2)=1\).

examples.title: Find the points, then identify the turns
examples.question: Find and classify every stationary point of \(g(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+2\) using first-derivative signs.
solution: The derivative is positive before \(-1\), negative between \(-1\) and \(3\), and positive after \(3\).
Thus \((-1,7)\) is a local maximum: increasing changes to decreasing. The point \((3,-25)\) is a local minimum: decreasing changes to increasing.

examples.title: Use the second derivative only at stationary inputs
examples.question: Find and classify the stationary points of \(h(x)=x^3+3x^2-9x+4\) using the second derivative.

examples.title: The same zero second derivative can lead to three outcomes
examples.question: Classify the stationary point at the origin for \(y=x^4\), \(y=-x^4\) and \(y=x^3\).
solution: All three first derivatives are zero at the origin. Their second derivatives, \(12x^2,-12x^2,6x\), are also zero there. This does not decide the nature.
For \(y=x^4\), the first derivative \(4x^3\) changes from negative to positive. The origin is a minimum.
For \(y=-x^4\), the first derivative \(-4x^3\) changes from positive to negative. The origin is a maximum.
For \(y=x^3\), the first derivative \(3x^2\) is positive on both sides. The origin is stationary but is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
The function \(x^3\) is strictly increasing throughout the real line. Its isolated zero gradient does not reverse or stop that overall increase.

examples.title: Compare stationary values and domain boundaries
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=6-(x-1)^2\) first on \([-1,4]\), then on \((-1,4)\).
solution:
The derivative is positive before \(1\) and negative after it. Compare the included endpoints as well:

\[f(-1)=2,\qquad f(4)=-3.\]

On the closed interval the minimum is \(-3\) and the maximum is \(6\). The function is continuous, so it takes every value between them:

\[\text{Range on }[-1,4]:\ [-3,6].\]

On the open interval the maximum \(6\) is still attained at \(x=1\). The lower bound \(-3\) is approached as \(x\) approaches \(4\), but is never attained:

\[\text{Range on }(-1,4):\ (-3,6].\]
Removing the input \(-1\) does not remove its output \(2\) from the range: \(f(3)=2\), and \(3\) remains in the domain.

examples.title: A local maximum need not be a global maximum
examples.question: Find all stationary points and the full range of \(f(x)=x+\frac{16}{x}\), \(x\ne0\).
solution: The denominator is positive on the domain. The derivative is positive for \(x<-4\) and \(x>4\), and negative for \(-4<x<0\) and \(0<x<4\).

On the negative component, the function tends to negative infinity toward either end, giving range \(( -\infty,-8]\). On the positive component, it tends to positive infinity toward either end, giving range \([8,\infty)\).
There is no global maximum or minimum on the full domain, because values are unbounded above and below. Zero is not a stationary input: it is excluded.

examples.title: A parameter can change the number and nature of stationary points
examples.question: For \(f_k(x)=x^3-3kx\), classify the stationary behaviour for every real \(k\). When is the function strictly increasing throughout the real line?
solution: If \(k<0\), there are no real stationary inputs. The derivative is positive everywhere, so the function is strictly increasing.
If \(k=0\), the only stationary point is \((0,0)\). It is neither a maximum nor a minimum, and the function \(x^3\) is strictly increasing.

If \(k>0\), there are two stationary inputs, \(x=\pm\sqrt{k}\). Since \(f_k^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x\), the negative input gives a maximum and the positive input gives a minimum:

\[(-\sqrt{k},\,2k\sqrt{k})\quad\text{maximum},\qquad(\sqrt{k},\,-2k\sqrt{k})\quad\text{minimum}.\]
For \(k>0\), the derivative is negative between the stationary inputs, so the function is not increasing throughout the real line. Therefore the complete condition for strict increase is \(k\le0\).

related.title: Derivatives, rational powers and the chain rule

extraPractice.title: Recover both coordinates and classify each stationary point
extraPractice.prompt: Find all stationary points of \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\). Classify them from left to right, and choose the set where \(f^{\prime}(x)<0\).
extraPractice.hint: Factor the derivative and read its sign on all three intervals. Use the original function for the heights.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3).\]

  2. The stationary inputs are \(1,3\). Their heights are \(f(1)=5\) and \(f(3)=1\).

  3. The derivative signs are positive for \(x<1\), negative for \(1<x<3\), and positive for \(x>3\). Therefore \((1,5)\) is a local maximum and \((3,1)\) is a local minimum.

  4. The strict derivative inequality excludes both zero-derivative endpoints: \(1<x<3\).

extraPractice.title: A zero second derivative does not rule out a minimum
extraPractice.prompt: For \(f(x)=(x-2)^4-3\), give the stationary point, the value of \(f^{\prime\prime}\) there, and its nature.

fields.label: Second derivative at the stationary input

options.neither: Neither a maximum nor a minimum

extraPractice.hint: Use the sign of \(4(x-2)^3\) on each side of the stationary input. Do not stop when the second derivative is zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=4(x-2)^3=0\Longrightarrow x=2,\qquad f(2)=-3.\]
  2. \[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12(x-2)^2,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(2)=0.\]

  3. The second-derivative test is inconclusive. The first derivative changes from negative to positive at \(2\), so \((2,-3)\) is a local minimum. In fact, \((x-2)^4\ge0\) makes it a global minimum as well.

extraPractice.title: Distinguish a strict derivative inequality from strict increase
extraPractice.prompt: For \(f(x)=(x+1)^3-2\), identify the nature of its stationary point. Choose the set where \(f^{\prime}(x)>0\), and decide whether \(f\) is strictly increasing on the whole real line.

options.neither: Neither a maximum nor a minimum

fields.label: Strictly increasing on the whole real line?

extraPractice.hint: The derivative is a nonnegative square with one zero. The cubic still rises through its horizontal tangent.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3(x+1)^2,\qquad f^{\prime}(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow x=-1.\]

  2. The stationary point is \((-1,-2)\). The derivative is positive on both sides, so there is no local maximum or minimum.

  3. The set where the derivative is strictly positive excludes \(-1\). However, the function is strictly increasing on the whole real line: translating the input and output of a strictly increasing cubic preserves strict increase.

extraPractice.title: Compare stationary values with both included endpoints
extraPractice.prompt: Find the minimum and maximum values of \(f(x)=-x^2+6x+1\) on \(0\le x\le5\). Give the input where each occurs.
extraPractice.hint: Check the interior stationary input and both domain endpoints. The global minimum need not have zero derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=-2x+6=0\Longrightarrow x=3.\]
  2. \[f(0)=1,\qquad f(3)=10,\qquad f(5)=6.\]

  3. The minimum is \(1\) at \(x=0\); the maximum is \(10\) at \(x=3\). The function is continuous on the whole closed interval, so its range is \([1,10]\).

extraPractice.title: An open input boundary can give an unattained output bound
extraPractice.prompt: Find the range of \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\) for \(0<x<3\). Enter the lower and upper bounds and choose which are attained.
extraPractice.hint: The vertex is inside the interval. Examine both open ends, and check whether any other allowed input gives the largest limiting value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=2(x-2),\qquad f(2)=1.\]

  2. The minimum \(1\) is attained at the allowed input \(2\). As \(x\) approaches zero from the right, \(f(x)\) approaches \(5\); as \(x\) approaches \(3\) from the left, it approaches \(2\).

  3. \[f(x)=5\Longleftrightarrow(x-2)^2=4\Longleftrightarrow x=0\text{ or }x=4.\]

  4. Neither input is allowed, so \(5\) is not attained. All outputs between \(1\) and \(5\) occur on the continuous branch from the left boundary to the vertex. The range is \([1,5)\).

extraPractice.title: Keep the two components of a reciprocal curve separate
extraPractice.prompt: For \(f(x)=x+\frac{9}{x}\), where \(x\ne0\), give all stationary points and select the complete range.
extraPractice.hint: Solve the derivative equation on both sides of the excluded input. Determine the range of each branch separately.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=1-\frac{9}{x^2}=0\Longrightarrow x^2=9\Longrightarrow x=\pm3.\]

  2. The stationary points are \((-3,-6)\) and \((3,6)\). Since \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{18}{x^3}\), the negative-input point is a local maximum and the positive-input point is a local minimum.

  3. On the positive branch the function tends to positive infinity at both ends and has minimum \(6\). Its range is \([6,\infty)\). The negative branch has maximum \(-6\), tends to negative infinity at both ends, and has range \((-\infty,-6]\).

  4. \[\text{Full range}=(-\infty,-6]\cup[6,\infty).\]

  5. The excluded pole \(x=0\) is not a stationary point and does not connect the two branches.

starters.title: Stationary inputs determine a curve, but endpoints determine its full range
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+12x-7\). It has stationary points at inputs \(x=1\) and \(x=2\). Find \(a,b\), give the local maximum and minimum points, and find the range of the recovered function on \(0\le x\le3\).
starters.hint: Use the two zero-gradient conditions to find the parameters. Then classify the stationary points and compare their heights with both endpoint heights.
starters.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3ax^2+2bx+12.\]
  2. \[3a+2b+12=0,\qquad12a+4b+12=0.\]

  3. Subtract twice the first equation from the second: \(6a-12=0\). Thus \(a=2\), and the first equation gives \(b=-9\).

  4. \[f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x-7,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12x-18.\]

  5. At \(1\), the second derivative is \(-6\), giving a local maximum \((1,-2)\). At \(2\), it is \(6\), giving a local minimum \((2,-3)\).

  6. \[f(0)=-7,\quad f(1)=-2,\quad f(2)=-3,\quad f(3)=2.\]

  7. The global minimum and maximum on the restricted domain occur at the endpoints. Continuity gives the complete range \([-7,2]\). Both bounds are attained.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the first derivative with unknown parameters.
  • 1 mark: form both stationary-input equations.
  • 1 mark: solve for \(a=2,b=-9\).
  • 1 mark: obtain both complete stationary coordinates.
  • 1 mark: justify the local maximum at \(x=1\).
  • 1 mark: justify the local minimum at \(x=2\).
  • 1 mark: calculate and compare both endpoint values.
  • 1 mark: state the complete closed range \([-7,2]\).

starters.title: Include valid endpoints without calling them stationary
starters.question: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}\) on its full real domain, find all stationary points and their nature. Find every point where the global minimum is attained, then give the range bounds.
starters.hint: The square root gives a closed real domain. Its derivative is finite only inside that interval. Check the endpoint function values separately.
starters.solution:
1. \[9-x^2\ge0\Longrightarrow -3\le x\le3.\]
  2. \[f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\qquad(-3<x<3).\]

  3. The only finite zero derivative is at \(x=0\), giving \((0,3)\). The derivative changes from positive to negative there, so this is a local maximum and also the global maximum.

  4. \[f(-3)=f(3)=0.\]

  5. These endpoints give the global minimum but are not stationary points: they do not have a finite zero derivative. By continuity, the full range is \([0,3]\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: establish the real domain \([-3,3]\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the derivative and its interior domain.
  • 1 mark: find the sole stationary point \((0,3)\).
  • 1 mark: classify it using the derivative signs.
  • 1 mark: identify both endpoint minima without calling them stationary.
  • 1 mark: state the full range \([0,3]\).

starters.title: Separate parameter cases before using a stationary value
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=x^3-3kx+4\), where \(k\) is real. Choose the condition for two distinct stationary points, and the condition for strict increase on the entire real line. If the local maximum value is \(20\), find \(k\) and both stationary points.
starters.hint: The stationary equation is \(x^2=k\). For positive \(k\), classify the negative and positive roots before substituting into the function.
starters.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3(x^2-k),\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x.\]

  2. If \(k>0\), the two stationary inputs are \(-\sqrt{k}\) and \(\sqrt{k}\). They are a local maximum and minimum respectively. If \(k=0\), there is one stationary point with no maximum or minimum. If \(k<0\), there are none.

  3. For \(k<0\), the derivative is positive everywhere. For \(k=0\), the translated cubic is still strictly increasing despite its isolated zero derivative. For \(k>0\), the derivative is negative between the two stationary inputs. Thus strict increase on the whole real line occurs exactly when \(k\le0\).

  4. \[f(-\sqrt{k})=4+2k\sqrt{k}=20\Longrightarrow k\sqrt{k}=8\Longrightarrow k=4.\]
  5. \[f(-2)=20,\qquad f(2)=-12.\]

  6. The required points are the local maximum \((-2,20)\) and local minimum \((2,-12)\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the stationary equation \(x^2=k\).
  • 1 mark: distinguish the positive, zero and negative parameter cases.
  • 1 mark: give the strict-increase condition including \(k=0\).
  • 1 mark: identify the maximum branch and form its value equation.
  • 1 mark: solve for \(k=4\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete local maximum point.
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete local minimum point.

revision.body:
Use signs for direction, coordinates for points and the full domain for the range.

Signs and stationary points

Find \(f^{\prime}\), mark its zeros and undefined points, then test every interval. Positive derivative gives increase; negative gives decrease. Solve \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\), retain allowed inputs, then calculate \((a,f(a))\).

Strict increase can include an isolated zero gradient. Keep disconnected domain components separate.

Classify an isolated stationary point

First derivative changes positive to negative: maximum; negative to positive: minimum; same nonzero sign: neither.

\[f^{\prime\prime}(a)>0:\ \text{minimum};\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(a)<0:\ \text{maximum}.\]

Use this only after \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\). If \(f^{\prime\prime}(a)=0\), use the first-derivative sign test.

Find the whole range

Compare interior stationary values, included endpoints and any other allowed points where the derivative is undefined. At open or unbounded ends, check the values approached. Include a bound only if some allowed input attains it. Combine ranges of separate components.

Local extrema need not be global. A boundary extreme need not be stationary.

Keep every parameter case

\[f_k(x)=x^3-3kx,\qquad f_k^{\prime}(x)=3(x^2-k).\]

For \(k<0\): no stationary points. For \(k=0\): one, with no turn. For \(k>0\): two, at \(\pm\sqrt{k}\). Strict increase on the real line holds for \(k\le0\). A vertical shift changes heights, not derivative signs.
revision.checks:
• Original domain retained?
  • Every stationary point has coordinates and a reason for its nature?
  • Endpoints and unattained bounds checked?
  • Equality and all parameter branches included?

orig_differentiation_rates.description: Connect changing quantities with the chain rule, keep signs and units, then use a starting gradient to estimate small changes and percentage errors.

sections.title: What is changing, and what does its rate mean?
sections.label: Signs and units
sections.intro: A rate tells you how fast one quantity changes relative to another. With time \(t\), \(\frac{dr}{dt}\) is a radius rate, while \(\frac{dV}{dt}\) is a volume rate. These are different quantities with different units. A finite ratio \(\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta t}\) is an average rate over an interval; it need not equal the instantaneous rate \(\frac{dV}{dt}\).

blocks.html:
Increasing gives a positive signed rate; decreasing gives a negative one. “Shrinks at \(2\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\)” means \(\frac{dr}{dt}=-2\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). The speed of that decrease is the positive magnitude.

For lengths in centimetres and time in seconds, length, area and volume rates have units \(\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}\) and \(\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.title: Convert the time unit before combining flows
blocks.prompt: A tank receives water at \(0.72\ \mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}\) and loses water at \(20\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\). Find its signed volume rate in \(\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\), then state whether the volume rises or falls.
blocks.hint: Use \(1\ \mathrm{L}=1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) and \(1\ \mathrm{min}=60\ \mathrm{s}\). Net rate is inflow minus outflow.
blocks.solution:
1. \[0.72\ \mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}=\frac{720}{60}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}=12\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}.\]
  2. \[\frac{dV}{dt}=12-20=-8\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}.\]

  3. The negative sign means the volume falls.

blocks.html: Do not add a per-minute flow to a per-second flow. Convert both quantity and time units first. For a container, use net inflow minus outflow, not the inflow alone.

sections.title: How do I connect two rates at the same instant?
sections.label: The rate chain
sections.intro: If \(y=f(x)\) and \(x\) changes with time, the chain rule connects the rates. Differentiate the relationship before substituting the particular instant’s values.

blocks.html:
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}.\]

Evaluate every factor at the same instant. If \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is finite and nonzero, you may rearrange:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dy}{dx}}.\]

blocks.title: Recover the input rate from the output rate
blocks.prompt: A point has coordinates in centimetres and moves on \(y=x^3+2x\). At an instant when \(x=2\), its vertical coordinate increases at \(21\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\frac{dx}{dt}\).
blocks.hint: At the same instant, evaluate \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+2\), then use the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=14.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}\Longrightarrow21=14\frac{dx}{dt}.\]
  3. \[\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{3}{2}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]

blocks.html: For a longer chain, multiply derivatives in order through the intermediate variables. If several outputs depend on the same changing length, calculate the length rate once and use it in each output formula.

You cannot invert a zero derivative. For \(y=x^2\) at \(x=0\), any finite \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) gives \(\frac{dy}{dt}=0\); knowing this zero output rate does not determine the input rate. If a nonzero output rate is prescribed there, it is incompatible with a finite input rate in this model.
Write the derivative chain before inserting numbers. It shows which rate you need, which rate you know and which derivative connects them.

sections.title: How do I turn a geometry description into one changing variable?
sections.label: Geometry and constraints
sections.intro: Write the geometric relationship and identify which dimensions are fixed. Useful formulas are \(A=\pi r^2\) and \(C=2\pi r\) for a circle, \(V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\) for a sphere, and \(V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h\) for a cone. A diameter \(d=2r\) also gives \(\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{dd}{dt}\).

blocks.html: At \(r=4\), the sphere has \(\frac{dV}{dr}=64\pi\). The volume rate \(32\pi\) therefore gives a radius rate of \(\frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.title: A shrinking radius gives a negative area rate
blocks.prompt: A circle has radius \(5\ \mathrm{cm}\), decreasing at \(0.3\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find the signed area rate in \(\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}\). Give an exact answer.
blocks.hint: Use \(A=\pi r^2\) and \(\frac{dr}{dt}=-0.3\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r,\qquad \frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}.\]
  2. \[\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi(5)(-0.3)=-3\pi\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}.\]

blocks.html: If two dimensions change together, use their constraint to express the target quantity in one variable before differentiating. Similar triangles, a fixed perimeter or Pythagoras can supply that relationship. A dimension’s value at one instant is not a constant for the whole motion.

blocks.title: Use the fixed perimeter before differentiating
blocks.prompt: A rectangle has fixed perimeter \(40\ \mathrm{cm}\). Its sides are \(x\) and \(y\). When \(x=6\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(x\) increases at \(0.4\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find the signed rates of change of \(y\) and the area \(A\).
blocks.hint: Write \(y=20-x\) and \(A=x(20-x)\), then connect their derivatives with \(\frac{dx}{dt}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[y=20-x,\qquad\frac{dy}{dx}=-1\Longrightarrow\frac{dy}{dt}=-0.4\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]
  2. \[A=20x-x^2,\qquad\frac{dA}{dx}=20-2x.\]
  3. \[\frac{dA}{dt}=(20-12)(0.4)=3.2=\frac{16}{5}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}.\]

blocks.html: In a filling cone, the water-surface radius changes with depth. Replacing it by a single measured radius before differentiation loses that change. Keep physical restrictions such as positive lengths and depths within the container.

sections.title: How does an instantaneous rate estimate a small change?
sections.label: Changes and new values
sections.intro: An instantaneous rate is exact at the stated instant. Multiplying it by a finite change gives a local estimate, because the rate may vary during that change. Let the input move from \(a\) to \(a+\Delta x\).

blocks.html:
\[\Delta y=f(a+\Delta x)-f(a)\approx f^{\prime}(a)\Delta x.\]\[f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)\Delta x.\]

The first formula estimates the change; the second estimates the new value. Use the derivative at the starting input and preserve the sign of \(\Delta x\).
Near \(x=3\), the tangent to \(y=x^2\) predicts the new value \(9+6h\). The curve’s exact value is \(9+6h+h^2\).

blocks.title: Find the estimated change before the new value
blocks.prompt: Use differentiation at \(x=2\) to estimate \((2.01)^3\). Give the estimated change in \(y=x^3\), then the estimated new value.
blocks.hint: The input change is \(0.01\). Multiply it by the derivative at the starting input, then add the old output.

blocks.html: The same idea estimates a change over a short time: \(\Delta y\approx\left.\frac{dy}{dt}\right|_{\text{start}}\Delta t\). Add this to the starting value. Do not assume a rate stays constant throughout a finite time interval unless the model says so.

Keep the new input inside the original domain. A small numerical step alone does not guarantee a stated accuracy. At a stationary input the estimate may be zero while the true change is not: from zero to \(0.1\), \(x^2\) changes by \(0.01\). Use an exact comparison or justified error bound when accuracy matters.

sections.title: How do I estimate percentage changes and measurement errors?
sections.label: Relative and percentage changes
sections.intro: For nonzero starting value \(y=f(a)\), the relative change is \(\frac{\Delta y}{y}\); multiply by \(100\%\) for percentage change. For positive measured quantities, define the signed measurement error as measured value minus true value. A negative error means the measurement is too low.

blocks.html:
\[\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx\frac{f^{\prime}(a)}{f(a)}\Delta x.\]

For a power relationship \(y=Cx^n\), with nonzero real values in its domain,

\[\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx n\frac{\Delta x}{x}.\]

Thus the small percentage output change is approximately \(n\) times the percentage input change. Negative powers can reverse the sign.

blocks.title: A positive input error can give a negative output error
blocks.prompt: For \(y=5x^{-2}\), \(x>0\), a measurement of \(x\) is \(0.6\%\) too high. Estimate the signed percentage error in the calculated \(y\), and its magnitude. Enter the numerical percentages.
blocks.hint: For a power \(y=Cx^n\), the small relative output error is approximately \(n\) times the relative input error.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx-2\frac{\Delta x}{x}.\]

  2. The signed percentage error is approximately \(-2(0.6\%)=-1.2\%\). The calculated value is too low; the magnitude of the percentage error is approximately \(1.2\%\).

blocks.html: When comparing an approximation with an exact value, state which difference you use. Here we normally use estimate minus exact value; if a question explicitly defines exact minus estimate, follow its stated order. Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference. For a signed percentage error, divide the chosen signed difference by the magnitude of the nonzero exact value and multiply by \(100\%\).

Distinguish a signed error from its magnitude, and an estimated change from an estimated new value. Keep \(\approx\) for the small-change calculation. The power multiplier gives a local approximation, not an exact rule for large percentage changes.

glossary.definition: How fast a quantity changes at one particular instant.
The combined signed rate; for a container, inflow minus outflow.
A relationship that remains true while the quantities change.
A signed change, such as \(\Delta x=\text{new input}-\text{old input}\).
An estimate using the tangent and its gradient at the starting point.
The change divided by the nonzero starting value.
An estimate or measurement minus the corresponding exact or true value.

examples.title: Use a signed net rate in consistent units
examples.question: Water enters a tank at \(0.9\ \mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}\) and leaks out at \(4\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\frac{dV}{dt}\) in \(\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\).
solution:
Convert the inflow to the same volume and time units as the leak:

\[0.9\ \mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}=\frac{900}{60}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}=15\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}.\]
The positive rate means that the water volume is increasing at that instant.

examples.title: Connect two coordinate rates at the same instant
examples.question: A point moves on \(y=x^2-3x+1\). First find \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) when \(x=4\) and \(\frac{dx}{dt}=-2\) units per second. At another instant, \(x=1\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt}=6\) units per second; find \(\frac{dx}{dt}\).
solution:
At the second instant the gradient is \(2(1)-3=-1\), so

\[6=-\frac{dx}{dt}\Longrightarrow\frac{dx}{dt}=-6\text{ units per second}.\]
Use the derivative and known rate from the same instant. The horizontal rate need not be constant between these two instants.

examples.title: Turn a volume rate into a radius rate
examples.question: A spherical balloon has volume \(V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\). At an instant when \(r=4\ \mathrm{cm}\), its volume increases at \(32\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\). Find the radius rate.
solution: The radius is increasing. The units also check: a volume rate divided by an area gives a length rate.

examples.title: Use similar triangles to connect both changing dimensions
examples.question: An inverted conical tank has height \(12\ \mathrm{cm}\) and top radius \(4\ \mathrm{cm}\). Water enters at a net rate of \(8\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\). When the water depth is \(6\ \mathrm{cm}\), find the rates of increase of the depth \(h\) and water-surface radius \(r\).
solution:
Similar triangles give a relationship that holds throughout the filling:

\[\frac{r}{h}=\frac{4}{12}=\frac{1}{3}\Longrightarrow r=\frac{h}{3}.\]

Eliminate the changing radius before differentiating:

\[V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h=\frac{\pi h^3}{27},\qquad\frac{dV}{dh}=\frac{\pi h^2}{9}.\]
The container’s dimensions stay fixed; the water’s depth and surface radius both change. The instant \(0<h<12\) is within the physical domain.

examples.title: Connect two lengths using a fixed constraint
examples.question: A \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) ladder rests against a vertical wall. Its foot is \(6\ \mathrm{m}\) from the wall and moves away at \(0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). How fast does the top move vertically?
solution:
Let \(x\) be the horizontal distance and \(y>0\) the height. Pythagoras gives

\[x^2+y^2=100\Longrightarrow y=\sqrt{100-x^2},\qquad0<x<10.\]
The signed vertical rate is negative. The top moves down at a speed of \(\frac{3}{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Compare a tangent estimate with the exact change
examples.question: Use differentiation to estimate the change in \(y=x^2\) as \(x\) increases from \(3\) to \(3.2\). Estimate the new value and compare it with the exact value.
solution:
The tangent estimate is too small by \(0.04\). In fact, for an input change \(h\),

\[(3+h)^2=9+6h+h^2.\]
The exact change is \(6h+h^2\), while the estimate retains \(6h\). The omitted term \(h^2\) explains the error for positive or negative \(h\).

examples.title: A decrease gives a negative increment
examples.question: Use differentiation at \(x=16\) to estimate \(\sqrt{15.84}\). Decide whether this estimate is above or below the exact value.
solution: Both the old and new inputs are positive, so the model remains in its domain. Since \((3.98)^2=15.8404>15.84\) and \(3.98>0\), the estimate \(3.98\) is slightly too high.

examples.title: Convert a small measurement error into a percentage output error
examples.question: A sphere’s measured radius is \(0.4\%\) too high. Estimate the signed percentage error in the volume calculated from this measurement.
solution:
Divide by the true starting volume:

\[\frac{\Delta V}{V}\approx\frac{4\pi r^2\Delta r}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}=3\frac{\Delta r}{r}.\]
The signed relative radius error is \(0.004\). Therefore the relative volume error is approximately \(0.012\), or \(+1.2\%\). The calculated volume is too high.

This is a first-order estimate. The exact percentage error is

\[\bigl((1.004)^3-1\bigr)\times100\%=1.2048064\%.\]

extraPractice.title: Keep the sign when connecting two rates
extraPractice.prompt: Two lengths, \(x\) and \(y\), are measured in centimetres and satisfy \(y=3x^2-5x\). At an instant when \(x=2\), the signed rate is \(\frac{dx}{dt}=-0.4\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) in centimetres per second.
extraPractice.hint: Calculate \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at the current input, then multiply by the signed input rate.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=6x-5,\qquad \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=7.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}=7(-0.4)=-2.8\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]

  3. The negative sign means the length \(y\) is decreasing at this instant.

extraPractice.title: Recover the input rate from a nonzero derivative
extraPractice.prompt: Lengths \(x,y\), measured in centimetres, satisfy \(y=\sqrt{4x+1}\). When \(x=2\), \(\frac{dy}{dt}=3\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) in centimetres per second.
extraPractice.hint: Write the chain equation first. Divide by the current derivative, which is nonzero here.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{4x+1}},\qquad \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  2. \[3=\frac{2}{3}\frac{dx}{dt}\Longrightarrow\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{9}{2}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]

extraPractice.title: A diameter rate must be converted to a radius rate
extraPractice.prompt: A spherical bubble has diameter \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\). Its diameter is decreasing at \(0.2\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\). Find the signed radius rate and the signed volume rate, in centimetres per second and cubic centimetres per second respectively.

retry.feedback: This is the diameter rate. Since \(d=2r\), the radius changes at half that signed rate.
The bubble is shrinking, so its signed volume rate is negative.

extraPractice.hint: Use \(d=2r\), so both the current radius and its rate are half the corresponding diameter quantities.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r=5\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}(-0.2)=-0.1\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]
  2. \[V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\Longrightarrow\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}.\]
  3. \[\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi(5)^2(-0.1)=-10\pi\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}.\]

extraPractice.title: Connect area, radius and circumference
extraPractice.prompt: A circular stain has radius \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\). Its area is decreasing at \(6\,\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}\). Find the signed radius rate and the signed circumference rate in centimetres per second.
extraPractice.hint: The area rate is negative. Use \(A=\pi r^2\) to find the radius rate, then \(C=2\pi r\) for the circumference rate.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt},\qquad -6=6\pi\frac{dr}{dt}.\]
  2. \[\frac{dr}{dt}=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]
  3. \[\frac{dC}{dt}=2\pi\frac{dr}{dt}=-2\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]

extraPractice.title: Estimate the change and then the new value
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) and a linear estimate about \(x=25\) to estimate \(\sqrt{25.4}\). Give the estimated change, the estimated new value, and whether this estimate lies above or below the true value.

retry.feedback: This is the estimated change. Add it to the original value \(5\) to estimate the new value.

extraPractice.hint: Use the derivative at the starting input. Add the estimated change to \(5\). To compare with the exact value, square the positive estimate.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(25)=5,\qquad f^{\prime}(25)=\frac{1}{10},\qquad\Delta x=0.4.\]
  2. \[\Delta y\approx\frac{1}{10}(0.4)=0.04,\qquad\sqrt{25.4}\approx5+0.04=5.04.\]

  3. Since \(5.04^2=25.4016>25.4\) and both values are positive, the estimate is above the true square root. This is a linear approximation, not an exact equality.

extraPractice.title: Keep the sign of an estimated percentage change
extraPractice.prompt: For \(y=x^{-2}\), the positive input increases from \(x=4\) by \(1\%\). Estimate the signed percentage change in \(y\) and the new value of \(y\) using first-order changes.
extraPractice.hint: For a power \(y=x^n\), the first-order relative change is \(n\) times the relative input change.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx-2\frac{\Delta x}{x}=-2(0.01)=-0.02.\]

  2. The estimated signed percentage change is \(-2\%\), so the output decreases.

  3. \[y_{\mathrm{old}}=\frac{1}{16},\qquad y_{\mathrm{new}}\approx\frac{1}{16}(0.98)=\frac{49}{800}.\]

  4. The exact output factor is \((1.01)^{-2}\), so the finite percentage change is not exactly \(-2\%\).

starters.title: Use similar triangles and net flow before connecting rates
starters.question:
A cone-shaped tank has height \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) and top radius \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\), with its vertex at the bottom. Liquid enters at \(8\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\) and leaks out at \(2\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\).

When the liquid depth is \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\), find the liquid-surface radius, the net volume rate, the rate of increase of depth, and the rate of increase of the circular liquid-surface area.
starters.hint: Similar triangles give \(r=\frac{h}{2}\). Substitute this relationship into the volume and area formulas before differentiating.
starters.solution:
1. \[\frac{r}{h}=\frac{6}{12}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad r=\frac{h}{2}.\]
  2. \[V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h=\frac{\pi h^3}{12},\qquad\frac{dV}{dt}=8-2=6\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}.\]
  3. \[\frac{dV}{dh}=\frac{\pi h^2}{4},\qquad6=\frac{\pi(4)^2}{4}\frac{dh}{dt}.\]
  4. \[r=2\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{3}{2\pi}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.\]
  5. \[A=\pi r^2=\frac{\pi h^2}{4},\qquad\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{\pi h}{2}\frac{dh}{dt}.\]
  6. \[\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi\frac{3}{2\pi}=3\,\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}.\]

  7. The surface radius varies with depth; the fixed tank-top radius is not the liquid radius at every depth.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain \(r=\frac{h}{2}\) and the current radius.
  • 1 mark: express the liquid volume in terms of depth alone.
  • 1 mark: use the net rate \(6\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\).
  • 1 mark: form the connected depth-rate equation.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{3}{2\pi}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\).
  • 1 mark: express and differentiate the surface area as a function of depth.
  • 1 mark: obtain the signed area rate with correct units.

starters.title: An instantaneous rate can change even when another speed stays constant
starters.question:
A rigid ladder of length \(13\,\mathrm{m}\) rests between a vertical wall and a horizontal floor. Its base moves away from the wall at a constant \(0.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Let \(x\) be the base distance and \(y\) the top height.

Find the signed top-height rate when \(x=5\), and again when \(x=12\). Starting from the instant \(x=5\), estimate the top height \(0.2\,\mathrm{s}\) later using the initial instantaneous rate.
starters.hint: Use \(y=\sqrt{169-x^2}\), then connect \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) to the constant base speed. Use the first height rate only for the requested short-time approximation.
starters.solution:
1. \[y=\sqrt{169-x^2},\qquad\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{169-x^2}}=-\frac{x}{y}.\]
  2. \[\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{x}{y}\frac{dx}{dt}.\]

  3. When \(x=5\), \(y=12\), so

    \[\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{5}{12}(0.6)=-\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]

  4. When \(x=12\), \(y=5\), so

    \[\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{12}{5}(0.6)=-\frac{36}{25}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]
  5. \[\Delta y\approx-\frac{1}{4}(0.2)=-0.05\,\mathrm{m},\qquad y_{\mathrm{new}}\approx12-0.05=11.95\,\mathrm{m}.\]

  6. The constant base speed does not make the top-height rate constant. The last result uses the initial rate as a short-time linear estimate; it is not the exact later height.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the length relationship and positive height expression.
  • 1 mark: form the connected top-height rate.
  • 1 mark: find the signed rate at base distance five metres.
  • 1 mark: find the signed rate at base distance twelve metres.
  • 1 mark: use the initial rate to estimate the short-time height change.
  • 1 mark: state the new height as an approximation with correct units.

starters.title: An affine inside expression changes the percentage multiplier
starters.question: Let \(y=(2x+1)^3\). The input increases by \(1\%\) from \(x=2\). Use differentiation to estimate the new value of \(y\) and its signed percentage change. Then calculate the exact value of \(y\) at the new input, and find the signed error defined as exact value minus linear estimate.
starters.hint: The input change is \(0.02\). The exponent alone is not the percentage multiplier for a power of \(2x+1\): first calculate the derivative and divide the estimated output change by the original output.
starters.solution:
1. \[y(2)=125,\qquad\frac{dy}{dx}=6(2x+1)^2,\qquad\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=150.\]
  2. \[\Delta x=0.01(2)=0.02,\qquad\Delta y\approx150(0.02)=3.\]
  3. \[y_{\mathrm{new}}\approx125+3=128,\qquad\frac{\Delta y}{125}\times100\%\approx2.4\%.\]
  4. \[x_{\mathrm{new}}=2.02,\qquad y_{\mathrm{exact}}=(5.04)^3=128.024064.\]
  5. \[\text{Signed error}=128.024064-128=0.024064.\]

  6. The positive error shows that this particular linear estimate is below the exact value. The estimated percentage change is not \(3\%\), because the inside expression is not simply \(x\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the derivative and its value at the initial input.
  • 1 mark: convert the input percentage into \(\Delta x=0.02\).
  • 1 mark: estimate \(\Delta y=3\) and hence the new value \(128\).
  • 1 mark: divide by the original output to estimate \(2.4\%\).
  • 1 mark: compute the exact later value \(128.024064\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the signed error using the stated convention.

revision.body:
Form the relationship first. Connect exact rates, or clearly label a finite-change estimate.

Signed rates and units

Increasing: positive rate. Decreasing: negative rate. A speed or error magnitude is nonnegative. Convert quantity and time units before combining rates. Net volume rate is inflow minus outflow.

Length, area and volume rates use \(\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\) when centimetres and seconds are used.

Connect rates at one instant

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}.\]

Use values from the same instant. Divide by the connecting derivative only when it is finite and nonzero. In geometry, use the fixed constraint to eliminate other changing dimensions, differentiate, then substitute the instant’s values. Check physical domains.

Estimate a small change and a new value

\[\Delta y\approx f^{\prime}(a)\Delta x,\qquad y_{\text{new}}\approx f(a)+\Delta y.\]

Use the starting gradient and signed input change. For a short time, use the starting time rate multiplied by \(\Delta t\). Keep the new input in the domain. A finite change is generally approximate, even when the instantaneous rate is exact.

Relative changes and errors

\[\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx\frac{f^{\prime}(a)}{f(a)}\Delta x.\]\[y=Cx^n:\qquad\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx n\frac{\Delta x}{x}.\]

Starting denominators must be nonzero. Multiply relative change by \(100\%\). Signed measurement error is measured minus true; its magnitude is nonnegative. The percentage multiplier is a small-change estimate, not an exact large-change rule.
revision.checks:
• Known rate, requested rate and units identified?
  • Constraint differentiated before inserting instant values?
  • Signs and physical domain checked?
  • Change, new value and error clearly distinguished?
revision.examTip: Change, new value and error clearly distinguished?

orig_differentiation_optimisation.description: Build a feasible model, prove the greatest or least value, and connect stationary points with transformed curves and parameter conditions.

sections.title: How do I turn a practical problem into one function?
sections.label: Build the objective
sections.intro: Optimisation means finding the greatest or least possible value under stated conditions. The objective is the quantity to improve, such as area, volume or cost. The constraint is the relationship that must remain true.

blocks.html:
1. Define the dimensions and write the constraint.
  2. Write the objective, then eliminate other variables.
  3. State the feasible domain using every physical restriction.
  4. Differentiate, find allowed stationary inputs and prove which gives the required optimum.
  5. Recover every requested dimension and the objective value, with units.
The fence constraint is \(2x+y=24\), so \(A=x(24-2x)\) on \(0<x<12\). The greatest area is \(72\ \mathrm{m^2}\).

blocks.title: Build the three-sided fence model
blocks.prompt: A rectangular enclosure uses a wall for one side and \(32\ \mathrm{m}\) of fencing for the other three. Let \(x\) be each side perpendicular to the wall and \(y\) the remaining fenced side. Find the dimensions giving the greatest area and that area.
blocks.hint: Use \(2x+y=32\), then write the area in terms of \(x\) alone.
blocks.solution:
1. \[y=32-2x,\qquad A=x(32-2x),\qquad0<x<16.\]
  2. \[A^{\prime}(x)=32-4x=0\Longrightarrow x=8.\]
  3. \[y=16\ \mathrm{m},\qquad A=128\ \mathrm{m^2}.\]

  4. The identity \(A=128-2(x-8)^2\) proves this is the greatest possible area, and both dimensions are positive.

blocks.html: The constraint is not automatically the quantity to differentiate. A fixed perimeter supplies a relationship; it is the area or other requested objective that you maximise or minimise.

sections.title: How do I prove that a value is the global optimum?
sections.label: Feasibility and proof
sections.intro: A zero derivative identifies a possible interior optimum. It does not by itself prove that the point is allowed, that it has the right nature or that no better value occurs elsewhere.

blocks.html:
On a closed interval, compare the objective at every allowed interior stationary input, both endpoints, and any allowed interior point where the derivative is undefined. For open or unbounded ends, inspect limiting behaviour and whether a best bound is actually attained.

A derivative sign pattern over the whole feasible interval can prove the global result: increasing then decreasing gives a maximum; decreasing then increasing gives a minimum.

blocks.title: A boundary can be optimal without being stationary
blocks.prompt: Find the maximum value of \(F(x)=x(18-x)\) on \(0\le x\le6\), and the input where it occurs.
blocks.hint: The unrestricted stationary input is \(9\). Check whether it is allowed, then inspect the derivative on the actual interval.
blocks.solution:
1. \[F^{\prime}(x)=18-2x=0\Longrightarrow x=9,\quad\text{outside the domain}.\]

  2. On \([0,6]\), the derivative is positive, so the function is increasing. Its maximum occurs at the included right endpoint.

  3. \[F(6)=6(12)=72.\]

blocks.html: A nonzero second derivative classifies a stationary point locally. To claim a global optimum, connect that result to the whole domain, for example using a complete sign argument, endpoint comparison or a direct inequality such as a completed square.
Write a conclusion in the terms of the question. If the best bound is approached but never attained, say that no maximum or minimum exists; do not report an excluded endpoint as an optimal design.

sections.title: How do I optimise cylinders and folded boxes?
sections.label: Geometry models
sections.intro: For a cylinder, \(V=\pi r^2h\) and the curved area is \(2\pi rh\). Add \(2\pi r^2\) for two circular ends, or \(\pi r^2\) for one base. A fixed volume lets you express \(h\) in terms of \(r\) before differentiating. If materials have different costs per unit area, multiply each area by its own cost first.

blocks.title: Count one circular base for an open cylinder
blocks.prompt: An open cylindrical container has volume \(8\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), one base and no lid. Find the radius, height and least surface area.
blocks.hint: Use \(h=\frac{8}{r^2}\) and \(S=\pi r^2+2\pi rh\), with \(r>0\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[S=\pi r^2+\frac{16\pi}{r},\qquad S^{\prime}(r)=2\pi r-\frac{16\pi}{r^2}.\]
  2. \[S^{\prime}(r)=0\Longrightarrow r^3=8\Longrightarrow r=2.\]

  3. The derivative is negative below \(2\) and positive above it, so this is the global minimum on \(r>0\).

  4. \[h=\frac{8}{4}=2\ \mathrm{cm},\qquad S=4\pi+8\pi=12\pi\ \mathrm{cm^2}.\]

blocks.html: Count the physical faces carefully. A container without a lid has one circular base, not two. A stated dimension at a possible optimum is not a fixed constant during differentiation.

For a box made by cutting squares from a sheet, each base dimension loses twice the cut size. Write all three dimensions before multiplying them. The smallest original sheet dimension determines the upper bound on the cut.
A “show that” part asks you to justify the objective from the geometry. If that derivation stalls, a formula supplied in the question can still be used for the later differentiation part.

sections.title: How do transformations move stationary points and gradients?
sections.label: Transform the curve
sections.intro: Suppose \(g(x)=Af(Bx)+C\), where \(A\ne0\) and \(B\ne0\). To reproduce an original input \(a\), solve \(Bx=a\). Transform the height separately.

blocks.html:
\[(a,f(a))\mapsto\left(\frac{a}{B},\,Af(a)+C\right).\]\[g^{\prime}(x)=ABf^{\prime}(Bx),\qquad g^{\prime\prime}(x)=AB^2f^{\prime\prime}(Bx).\]

A positive \(A\) preserves maxima and minima; a negative \(A\) swaps them. A negative \(B\) reverses left and right, but does not by itself swap the nature. The new domain consists of inputs for which \(Bx\) lies in the original domain.
The minimum \((2,3)\) of \(f\) maps to the maximum \(\left(\frac{2}{3},-1\right)\) of \(g(x)=-2f(3x)+5\).

blocks.title: Separate the effects of horizontal and vertical factors
blocks.prompt: The graph of a differentiable function \(f\) has a local maximum at \((-3,4)\), and \(f^{\prime}(2)=-4\). Let \(g(x)=3f(-2x)-5\). Find the image of that point, classify it and calculate \(g^{\prime}(-1)\).
blocks.hint: Set \(-2x=-3\) for the mapped input. Heights become \(3f-5\), while derivatives acquire both factors.
blocks.solution:
1. \[x=\frac{3}{2},\qquad g(x)=3(4)-5=7.\]

  2. The positive vertical factor preserves a maximum. The negative inner factor reverses left and right, but not the type of extreme.

  3. \[g^{\prime}(x)=-6f^{\prime}(-2x),\qquad g^{\prime}(-1)=-6f^{\prime}(2)=24.\]

blocks.html: The input coordinate is divided by \(B\), while a derivative is multiplied by \(B\). Keep both factors in \(ABf^{\prime}(Bx)\). For classification, the second derivative contains \(AB^2\), so the sign of \(B\) disappears.

The nonzero assumptions matter. If \(A=0\), the expression is constant only on its inherited domain: excluded inputs of \(f(Bx)\) stay excluded. If \(B=0\), the expression requires \(f(0)\) to exist; when it does, \(g\) is constant. These cases do not give a one-to-one mapping of isolated stationary points.

sections.title: How do several point and gradient conditions determine parameters?
sections.label: Linked conditions
sections.intro: Translate each statement into its own equation. A point supplies a function value; a stationary input supplies a zero derivative. A prescribed gradient supplies a derivative value. Solve the resulting equations together, then verify the requested nature and domain.

blocks.html:
\[\text{Stationary point }(a,b):\qquad f(a)=b,\quad f^{\prime}(a)=0.\]

A minimum or maximum also needs a classification check. For a transformed curve, combine the input mapping, transformed height and derivative formula; a vertical shift changes the height but contributes zero to the derivative.

blocks.title: Use the height and the zero gradient together
blocks.prompt: The curve \(y=x^2+ax+b\) has a minimum at \((-2,3)\). Find \(a,b\).
blocks.hint: Use the stated point in the function and the stationary input in the derivative.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=2x+a,\qquad f^{\prime}(-2)=0\Longrightarrow a=4.\]
  2. \[f(-2)=4-2a+b=3\Longrightarrow b=7.\]

  3. The second derivative is \(2>0\), so the point is indeed a minimum. Both original conditions hold.

blocks.title: Combine transformed coordinates with a gradient condition
blocks.prompt: A differentiable function \(f\), defined for all real inputs, has a local minimum at \((3,4)\) and \(f^{\prime}(0)=5\). In \(g(x)=Af(Bx)+C\), where \(A,B\ne0\), this point maps to \((-1,-2)\), and \(g^{\prime}(0)=30\). Find \(A,B,C\) and classify the mapped stationary point.
blocks.hint: The input mapping fixes \(B\). Then use \(g^{\prime}(0)=ABf^{\prime}(0)\), followed by the mapped height.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{3}{B}=-1\Longrightarrow B=-3.\]
  2. \[30=AB(5)=-15A\Longrightarrow A=-2.\]
  3. \[-2=A(4)+C=-8+C\Longrightarrow C=6.\]

  4. Since \(A<0\), the original minimum becomes a local maximum. The negative \(B\) changes the horizontal position, not this classification.

blocks.html: Check every original condition after finding the parameters. Use the original function for the height, its derivative for the gradient and the full feasible domain for a global claim. Keep any separate solutions until the stated restrictions rule them out.

glossary.definition: The quantity whose greatest or least value is required.
A relationship or restriction that every allowed solution must satisfy.
All input values allowed by the model and its physical conditions.
The greatest or least attained value over the whole feasible domain.
Produced by at least one allowed input, rather than only approached.
The equation \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) at an allowed interior input.
Several statements about the same function or parameters that must hold together.

examples.title: Choose one variable for a constrained area
examples.question: A wall forms one side of a rectangular enclosure. There are \(24\ \mathrm{m}\) of fencing for the other three sides. Find the dimensions giving the greatest area.
solution:
Let \(x\) be each side perpendicular to the wall and \(y\) the remaining fenced side.

\[2x+y=24\Longrightarrow y=24-2x.\]

Positive side lengths give \(0<x<12\). The area is

\[A=xy=x(24-2x)=24x-2x^2.\]
The identity \(A=72-2(x-6)^2\) shows that no allowed input gives a greater value. Equality is attained at the feasible dimensions \(6\ \mathrm{m}\) by \(12\ \mathrm{m}\).

examples.title: Reject an infeasible stationary input and check attainment
examples.question: Find the greatest and least values of \(F(x)=12-(x-2)^2\) on \([4,7]\). What changes if the domain is \([4,7)\)?
solution: The stationary input is outside both stated domains. On either domain, \(F^{\prime}(x)<0\), so \(F\) is strictly decreasing.
On \([4,7]\), the maximum is \(8\) at \(x=4\) and the minimum is \(-13\) at \(x=7\).
On \([4,7)\), the maximum \(8\) is still attained. There is no minimum: values approach \(-13\) as \(x\) approaches \(7\), but no allowed input produces \(-13\).

examples.title: Minimise the surface area of a closed cylinder
examples.question: A closed cylindrical can has volume \(54\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\). Find the positive radius and height that minimise its total surface area, and calculate that area. Ignore material thickness.
solution:
Count two circular ends and the curved surface:

\[S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi r^2+\frac{108\pi}{r}.\]

For \(0<r<3\), the derivative is negative; for \(r>3\), it is positive. The surface area therefore decreases to this point and then increases throughout the remaining domain. This is a global minimum.

examples.title: Removing the lid changes the optimum
examples.question: An open cylindrical container has volume \(27\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), one base and no lid. Find the dimensions that minimise the material area.
solution: The derivative is negative before \(3\) and positive after it, so this is the global minimum on the physical domain.
Here the best height equals the radius. The closed can above has height twice its radius. These relationships come from the counted surfaces; rebuild the objective if faces or material costs change.

examples.title: Keep all dimensions positive in a folded-box model
examples.question: A square sheet has side \(12\ \mathrm{cm}\). Equal squares of side \(x\) are removed from its corners, and the sides are folded up to form an open box. Find the cut size giving the greatest volume.
solution:
The height is \(x\); each base side is \(12-2x\). Positive dimensions require \(0<x<6\).

\[V=x(12-2x)^2=144x-48x^2+4x^3.\]
The derivative vanishes at \(2\) and \(6\). Reject \(6\), which would give a zero-width base and is outside the feasible domain.
The derivative is positive on \((0,2)\) and negative on \((2,6)\). The volume tends to zero at both domain ends, so \(x=2\) gives the global maximum.

examples.title: Map a stationary point through a combined transformation
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+3\) and \(g(x)=-2f(3x)+5\). Find the stationary point of \(g\), classify it and check using differentiation.
solution:
The minimum of \(f\) is \((2,3)\). Set the transformed input equal to the original input:

\[3x=2\Longrightarrow x=\frac{2}{3}.\]
The negative vertical factor turns the minimum into a maximum, so the image is \(\left(\frac{2}{3},-1\right)\).

\[g^{\prime}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=0,\qquad g^{\prime\prime}(x)=-36<0.\]

The derivative check confirms the maximum.

examples.title: A negative inner factor reverses positions, not peak types
examples.question: The function \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) has a local maximum at \((-1,2)\) and a local minimum at \((1,-2)\). Find and classify the stationary points of \(g(x)=-2f(-3x)+5\).
solution:
Divide original inputs by \(-3\), and transform each height by multiplying by \(-2\) then adding \(5\):

\[(-1,2)\mapsto\left(\frac{1}{3},1\right),\qquad(1,-2)\mapsto\left(-\frac{1}{3},9\right).\]

The negative inner factor reverses left and right. The negative outer factor swaps maxima and minima. Thus \(\left(\frac{1}{3},1\right)\) is a local minimum and \(\left(-\frac{1}{3},9\right)\) is a local maximum.

\[g^{\prime\prime}(x)=324x.\]

It is positive at \(\frac{1}{3}\) and negative at \(-\frac{1}{3}\), confirming both classifications.

examples.title: A prescribed minimum gives two linked equations
examples.question: For \(x>0\), the curve \(f(x)=ax^2+\frac{b}{x}\) has a minimum at \((2,12)\). Find \(a,b\) and verify the minimum.
solution:
The stationary input gives a different condition:

\[f^{\prime}(x)=2ax-\frac{b}{x^2},\qquad4a-\frac{b}{4}=0\Longrightarrow b=16a.\]
Both original conditions hold. Also \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2(x^3-8)}{x^2}\) is negative before \(2\) and positive after it throughout \(x>0\), so the point is a global minimum on this domain.
