extraPractice.title: Turn a fixed perimeter into a one-variable area
extraPractice.prompt: A rectangle with positive side lengths has perimeter \(36\,\mathrm{m}\). Find its dimensions when its area is greatest, and find that greatest area.
extraPractice.hint: Let one side be \(x\). The other is \(18-x\), with \(0<x<18\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A(x)=x(18-x)=18x-x^2\qquad(0<x<18).\]
  2. \[A^{\prime}(x)=18-2x=0\Longrightarrow x=9.\]

  3. The derivative is positive before \(9\) and negative after \(9\) throughout the feasible interval, so this is the global maximum.

  4. \[18-x=9\,\mathrm{m},\qquad A_{\max}=9\times9=81\,\mathrm{m^2}.\]

extraPractice.title: A feasible boundary can beat every interior candidate
extraPractice.prompt:
A rectangular enclosure uses an existing wall for one side. The other three sides use \(60\,\mathrm{m}\) of fencing. Each perpendicular side has length \(x\), and a site restriction requires \(0<x\le10\).

Find the width \(x\), the side parallel to the wall, and the greatest possible area.
extraPractice.hint: The unconstrained stationary input lies outside the permitted interval. Check how the area changes throughout the actual interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[2x+y=60\Longrightarrow y=60-2x,\qquad A(x)=60x-2x^2.\]
  2. \[A^{\prime}(x)=60-4x=0\Longrightarrow x=15.\]

  3. This stationary input is not feasible. On \(0<x\le10\), the derivative is positive, so the area increases up to the included boundary \(x=10\).

  4. \[y=60-20=40\,\mathrm{m},\qquad A=10(40)=400\,\mathrm{m^2}.\]

extraPractice.title: An excluded limiting value is not an attained optimum
extraPractice.prompt: For \(F(x)=x^2+1\) with \(1<x<3\), find the lower and upper limiting bounds of the output. Decide whether either bound is attained.
extraPractice.hint: The function is strictly increasing on the stated interval, whose two endpoints are excluded.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[F^{\prime}(x)=2x>0\qquad(1<x<3).\]

  2. As \(x\) approaches \(1\) from above, \(F(x)\) approaches \(2\). As \(x\) approaches \(3\) from below, it approaches \(10\).

  3. The range is \((2,10)\). Every allowed value can be improved in either direction, so there is no attained minimum or maximum.

extraPractice.title: Transform coordinates, the domain and the nature of stationary points
extraPractice.prompt:
A differentiable function \(f\) has domain \([-2,4]\). Its only stationary points are a local maximum at \((2,5)\) and a local minimum at \((-1,-3)\). Define \(g(x)=-2f(3x)+7\).

Give the local maximum and minimum points of \(g\), and the bounds of its domain.

fields.label: Local maximum of the transformed curve
Local minimum of the transformed curve

extraPractice.hint: A point \((u,v)\) becomes \(\left(\frac{u}{3},-2v+7\right)\). The negative outside multiplier reverses maximum and minimum.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[g^{\prime}(x)=-6f^{\prime}(3x).\]

  2. The original minimum \((-1,-3)\) becomes the local maximum \(\left(-\frac{1}{3},13\right)\). The original maximum \((2,5)\) becomes the local minimum \(\left(\frac{2}{3},-3\right)\).

  3. \[-2\le3x\le4\Longrightarrow-\frac{2}{3}\le x\le\frac{4}{3}.\]

  4. Both domain endpoints remain included. The horizontal input scale changes locations, while the negative vertical scale changes the classifications.

extraPractice.title: The transformed gradient needs both scale factors
extraPractice.prompt: You are given \(f^{\prime}(-2)=3\). If \(g(x)=4f(-2x)+1\), find \(g^{\prime}(1)\).

retry.feedback: You included the outside factor. The chain rule also needs the inner factor \(-2\).
The inside factor is negative. Keep its sign when multiplying the derivative factors.

extraPractice.hint: The outer factor is \(4\), and the inside derivative is \(-2\). The vertical shift has derivative zero.

extraPractice.title: Use a point condition and a stationary condition separately
extraPractice.prompt: The curve \(f(x)=ax^3+bx+1\) passes through \((1,-2)\), which is a stationary point. Find \(a,b\), classify this point, and find the other stationary point.
extraPractice.hint: The height condition uses \(f(1)\), while the stationary condition uses \(f^{\prime}(1)=0\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[a+b+1=-2,\qquad f^{\prime}(x)=3ax^2+b,\qquad3a+b=0.\]

  2. Subtracting \(a+b=-3\) from \(3a+b=0\) gives \(2a=3\). Hence \(a=\frac{3}{2}\) and \(b=-\frac{9}{2}\).

  3. \[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{9}{2}(x^2-1),\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=9x.\]

  4. At \(x=1\), the second derivative is positive, so the given point is a local minimum. The other stationary input is \(-1\), giving height \(4\) and a negative second derivative; it is a local maximum at \((-1,4)\).

starters.title: Minimise the material in a closed cylinder
starters.question: A closed cylindrical container has volume \(128\pi\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). Its curved side and both circular ends use material of the same thickness. Find the radius and height that minimise its total surface area, and find the minimum surface area. Justify that the minimum is global for positive dimensions.
starters.hint: Use the volume constraint to eliminate height. A closed cylinder has two circular ends.
starters.solution:
1. \[\pi r^2h=128\pi\Longrightarrow h=\frac{128}{r^2}\qquad(r>0).\]
  2. \[S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi r^2+\frac{256\pi}{r}.\]
  3. \[S^{\prime}(r)=4\pi r-\frac{256\pi}{r^2}=\frac{4\pi(r^3-64)}{r^2}.\]
  4. \[S^{\prime}(r)=0\Longrightarrow r=4\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad h=\frac{128}{16}=8\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  5. For every positive radius below \(4\), the derivative is negative; for every radius above \(4\), it is positive. The area therefore decreases to this point and increases afterward, proving a global minimum.

  6. \[S_{\min}=2\pi(4)^2+2\pi(4)(8)=96\pi\,\mathrm{cm^2}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the volume constraint to express height in terms of radius.
  • 1 mark: form the total surface area including both ends.
  • 1 mark: differentiate the one-variable area correctly.
  • 1 mark: obtain the positive stationary radius \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  • 1 mark: restore the height \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  • 1 mark: justify the global minimum on the positive domain.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(96\pi\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

starters.title: Reject an algebraic root outside the physical box model
starters.question:
An open box is made from a \(30\,\mathrm{cm}\) by \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\) rectangular sheet. Equal squares of side \(x\) are cut from all four corners, and the remaining sides are folded upward.

Find the height, longer base side, shorter base side and greatest volume of the box. Give exact values and justify the maximum on the physical domain.
starters.hint: The dimensions are \(x\), \(30-2x\) and \(18-2x\). All must be positive, so use \(0<x<9\) before choosing a stationary root.
starters.solution:
1. \[V(x)=x(30-2x)(18-2x)=540x-96x^2+4x^3,\qquad0<x<9.\]
  2. \[V^{\prime}(x)=12(x^2-16x+45)=0\Longrightarrow x=8\pm\sqrt{19}.\]

  3. The input \(8+\sqrt{19}>9\) is infeasible. Only \(x=8-\sqrt{19}\) lies in the physical interval.

  4. The derivative is positive before this allowed input and negative after it throughout \((0,9)\). The volume approaches zero at both excluded degenerate ends, so the interior value is the global maximum.

  5. \[30-2x=14+2\sqrt{19},\qquad18-2x=2+2\sqrt{19}.\]
  6. \[V_{\max}=(8-\sqrt{19})(14+2\sqrt{19})(2+2\sqrt{19})=224+152\sqrt{19}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the volume in one variable.
  • 1 mark: state the strict physical domain \(0<x<9\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the derivative and its quadratic equation.
  • 1 mark: select \(8-\sqrt{19}\) and reject the infeasible root.
  • 1 mark: justify the global maximum over the whole feasible interval.
  • 1 mark: obtain the longer base side.
  • 1 mark: obtain the shorter base side.
  • 1 mark: give the exact greatest volume with correct units.

starters.title: Recover a transformation from linked point and gradient conditions
starters.question:
A twice differentiable function \(f\) has a stationary point at \((2,3)\), with \(f^{\prime}(0)=2\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(2)=-1\). Define \(g(x)=Af(Bx)+C\), where \(A,B\ne0\).

This stationary point is mapped to \((-1,-5)\) on \(g\), and \(g^{\prime}(0)=12\). Find \(A,B,C\), calculate \(g^{\prime\prime}(-1)\), and classify the transformed stationary point.
starters.hint: Match the inner input at the mapped point first. Use \(g^{\prime}(x)=ABf^{\prime}(Bx)\) for the gradient condition and \(g^{\prime\prime}(x)=AB^2f^{\prime\prime}(Bx)\) for the final classification.
starters.solution:
1. At the mapped contact, the inner input must equal \(2\):

    \[B(-1)=2\Longrightarrow B=-2.\]
  2. \[g^{\prime}(0)=ABf^{\prime}(0)=2AB=12\Longrightarrow AB=6\Longrightarrow A=-3.\]
  3. \[g(-1)=Af(2)+C=-5\Longrightarrow -9+C=-5\Longrightarrow C=4.\]
  4. \[g^{\prime\prime}(x)=AB^2f^{\prime\prime}(Bx).\]
  5. \[g^{\prime\prime}(-1)=(-3)(-2)^2(-1)=12.\]

  6. The mapped point is stationary because \(g^{\prime}(-1)=ABf^{\prime}(2)=0\). Its positive second derivative makes it a local minimum. The negative outside factor reverses the original maximum; the squared inside factor does not reverse this classification.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: match the original and transformed contact inputs.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(B=-2\).
  • 1 mark: form the gradient equation using both scale factors.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(A=-3\).
  • 1 mark: use the mapped height to obtain \(C=4\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the second derivative with the factor \(B^2\).
  • 1 mark: justify the local minimum at the stationary point.

revision.body:
An optimum needs a valid model, an allowed input and a proof over the full domain.

Build and reduce the model

Write the objective and constraint separately. Eliminate other variables and state all physical bounds before differentiating. For a cylinder, \(V=\pi r^2h\); curved area is \(2\pi rh\). Count two circular ends for a closed can, one for an open container.

For a cut-and-fold box, each base dimension loses twice the cut size.

Prove the global result

Keep only stationary inputs in the feasible domain. Compare included endpoints and any allowed points where the derivative is undefined. At open or unbounded ends, inspect limiting values and attainment.

A complete sign argument or direct bound can prove the global optimum. A second-derivative test alone gives a local classification. Report every requested dimension and value with units.

Transform points and derivatives

\[g(x)=Af(Bx)+C,\qquad A,B\ne0.\]\[(a,b)\mapsto\left(\frac{a}{B},Ab+C\right).\]\[g^{\prime}(x)=ABf^{\prime}(Bx),\qquad g^{\prime\prime}(x)=AB^2f^{\prime\prime}(Bx).\]

Negative \(A\) swaps maxima and minima. Negative \(B\) reverses positions. Require \(Bx\) to lie in the original domain.

Use linked conditions

A stationary point \((a,b)\) gives \(f(a)=b\) and \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\). A prescribed gradient uses the derivative. Combine mapped coordinates and gradients to determine transformation parameters.

Verify every original equation, the nature of the point and all domain restrictions. A bound at an excluded endpoint need not be attained.
revision.checks:
• Objective and constraint distinguished?
  • All dimensions and input bounds valid?
  • Global optimum proved, including relevant boundaries?
  • Transformed coordinates, chain factors and original conditions checked?
